items.body:
MONTHLY EDITORIAL
EINEN MOMENT BITTE!　横井一江
INTERVIEWS
NO. 341
ゴードン・グルディナ 〜 RU’YAについて語る
2026年9月19日
横井一江

text & photo by Kazue Yokoi  横井一江

ゴードン・グルディナは、バンクーバーを拠点に既成のジャンルにとらわれず世界的に活動するウード奏者／ギタリストで、ソロ・アルバム『China Cloud』でカナダ最高峰の音楽賞 Juno Awards の2019年度 Instrumental Album of the Year を受賞している。

子供の頃にギターを始めていたグルディナだが、13歳の時に初めてウードの演奏を聴き、衝撃を受ける。2002年にはウードの演奏も始めた。彼はまた20代の頃、ゲイリー・ピーコックに師事しており、最初の録音はゲイリー・ピーコック、ポール・モチアンとの『Think Like The Waves』（Songlines, 2006）。これまでフランソワ・ウール、ブノワ・デルベック、ハンク・ロバーツ、マシュー・シップ、武石聡、ケニー・ウィーラー、トニー・マラビーなどと共演。また、ジャンルにとらわれず幅広いミュージシャンと協働してきた彼は、ジャズ、即興演奏、ロック、アラブ音楽（マカーム）などを融合させた独自の音楽を演奏する。マット・ミッチェル Matt Mitchell (p) とジム・ブラック (ds) とのNomad Trio、The Marrow、Haramなどがそうだ。

2025年にグルディナは、RU’YAというプロジェクトを立ち上げる。そのステージを今年2026年のメールス・フェスティヴァルで観ることができた。RU’YAとは、アラビア語で「ビジョン」を意味するという。メンバーはグルディナ（g, oud, カナダ）、ガリア・ベナリ Ghalia Benali（vo, チュニジア）、Eylem Basaldi（vln, トルコ）、エリアス・セメスダー Elias Stemeseder（p, synth, オーストリア）、ハミン・ホラリ Hamin Honari（perc, イラン）、クリスチャン・リリンガー Christian Lillinger（ds, ドイツ）で、国籍もバックグラウンドも異なるメンバーからなる。アラブ音楽（マカーム）、ペルシア音楽、即興演奏などが融合することで織りなすサウンド、またベナリの存在によって詩やヴォイスが大きな要素として作用していた。パレスチナの詩人ナセル・ラバの詩が朗誦された。詩人の言葉は深い。会場にいるほとんどの人はアラビア語が分からないものの、発せられた言葉はサウンドとしてなにがしかを伝える。現在のパレスチナの情勢に抗する政治的なメッセージがあった。心に響く、音楽的にも稀に見るステージで、聴衆がスタンディング・オベイションで讃えていたのが印象的だった。

そこで、あらためてグルディナにRU’YAというプロジェクトについて、2度来日して道場（八木美知依、本田珠也）と巻上公一を初めとするミュージシャンと共演していることについても尋ねてみることにした。

 RU’YAについて

── RU’YAというプロジェクトを立ち上げた理由を教えてください。初演はベルリンのピエール・ブーレーズ・ザール（Pierre Boulez Saal）とのことですが、どのような経緯で公演に至ったのでしょうか。

自分が関心を持っている音楽の要素をすべて組み合わせ、活動しているさまざまなアンサンブルを繋ぐようなプロジェクトを作りたいと考えていました。自分が取り組んでいるすべての活動を、より包括的に表現できるプロジェクトを探していたのです。ピエール・ブーレーズ・ザールのピョートル・トルキエヴィチPiotr Turkiewicz と新しい委嘱作品のコンサートについて話し合っていた際、それを実現するための共演者について話題が及びました。この繋がりがきっかけとなり、プロジェクトを実現するための最適な環境と支援が得られることになったのです。

── とてもユニークな楽器編成のプロジェクトですが、どのような観点からこのような楽器編成にし、参加ミュージシャンを決めたのでしょうか。

私は普段からプロジェクトを立ち上げる際、楽器編成よりも「特定の人物」を中心に考えることが多いです。音楽的には、Nomad Trio（ノマド・トリオ）のために書いていた音楽と、自身のグループであるThe Marrow（ザ・マロウ）や Qalandar（カランダール）の要素を橋渡ししたいと考えていました。

また、ケベックのFIMAV（Festival International de Musique Actuelle de Victoriaville  ヴィクトリアヴィル国際現代音楽祭）で面白い体験がありました。主催者のミシェル・ルヴァスール Michel Levasseur が、私のグループであるSquare Peg（スクエア・ペグ）とThe Marrowのどちらを出演させるか決めきれず、結果として両グループが短めのセットを演奏した後、最後に合同の大型アンサンブルとして1つのセットを行ったのです。そこでクリスチャン（・リリンガー）とハミン（・ホナリ）が初めて共演しました。2人が融合したサウンドがとても気に入り、個人的にもすぐに意気投合していたことが大きな決め手となりました。

グループのリズムの核としてその2人を迎えたいと考えたほか、The Marrowと、モントリオール出身のConstantinople（コンスタンティノープル）、そしてガリア・ベナリによる対バン公演を行った際、彼女の地に足のついた、それでいて完全に自由なインプロヴィゼーション（即興演奏）の感覚と、マカーム（アラブ音楽の旋律法）の独自の使い方に魅了されました。彼女はこの新しいアンサンブルに最適だと確信しました。ハミン・ホナリはその夜、両方のアンサンブルで演奏しており、ガリアとも素晴らしい音楽的繋がりを持っていたのです。

私は、複雑な音楽を書く自由を持ちながら、それを美しく解釈し、理解してもらい、さらに別の人の音楽的言語を通して次のレベルへと発展させられるようにしたいと思っていました。それができるという点で、マット・ミッチェルは素晴らしい才能を持っています。私たちはそれまでにもかなり長いあいだ一緒に仕事をしてきたので、その関係を続けたいとも思っていました。

そこで、この二つの世界を橋渡しできるメロディ楽器の奏者を探していた際、バンクーバーでエイレム・バサルディ eylem Basaldi とトルステン・ミュラー Torsten Müller を加えたトリオで演奏したときに、とても素晴らしい経験をしました。彼女がトルコ音楽やアラブ音楽、そしてマカームについて幅広い知識を持っていることは知っていましたが、私たちがトリオで演奏したときは完全に自由な演奏で、実にさまざまな方向へ展開していきました。それが、とても魔法のような体験だったのです。

このグループなら、アーティスト同士の間にある程度の親しみを保ちながらも、まだ発見されていない領域を十分に残すことができ、そこからインスピレーションが生まれると思いました。そして、それぞれのミュージシャンから新しい表現の形を引き出せるのではないかと考えたのです。

── メールスではピアニストが初演時のマット・ミッチェル Matt Mitchell ではなく、クリスチャン・リリンガーとデュオでも活動しているエリアス・ステメゼダー Elias Stemeseder に変わりましたね。何か理由があったのでしょうか。

ピエール・ブーレーズ・ザールでのコンサートは素晴らしかったです。私たちは2セットとも非常に長い演奏をしましたが、観客は最後までずっとついてきてくれました！このプロジェクトを続けていきたいと思っていましたし、曲にはさらに練り上げる必要がありました。私たち自身も一緒に演奏する時間が必要だったので、その年の11月にカナダ・ツアーを組むことができたのは幸運でした。ただ、マットはそのツアーには参加できなかったんです。

ツアーのために誰に頼めばいいのか、私は途方に暮れました。マットは独自の技術を持っているだけでなく、アーティストとしての推進力や強さ、明確な個性を持っていますから。そこでマットがエリアスを推薦してくれました。私はクリスチャンとエリアスのデュオが大好きですし、以前にも何度か彼らと演奏したことがあって、とても楽しい時間を過ごしていました。エリアスはすでに、私が「もっと一緒に仕事をしたい」と心の中で思っていたアーティストでもあったのです。

エリアスはすぐにグループに溶け込み、ツアーの間にバンドは本当に一つにまとまっていきました。演奏する時間だけでなく一緒に過ごす時間もあったので、グループがまるで家族のように感じられるようになったのです。そしてツアーの最後にアルバムを録音しました。現在、そのリリースに向けた最終的な調整を行なっているところです。エリアスがシンセサイザーを加えたことで、プロジェクトに新しい次元がもたらされ、私はそれをとても嬉しく思っています。

── ジャズ、即興演奏、アラブ音楽、ペルシャ音楽といった全く異なるバックグラウンドを持つ音楽家たちがひとつのユニットで演奏するのは、とても難しいことのように思います。どのようにプロジェクトを発展させ、形作っていったのでしょうか。

ここに至るまでに、いくつかの要素が発展してきました。一つは、私がこれらすべての音楽の世界で長年活動してきたため、自分の中の音楽的な耳（心の内耳）において、それらをそれほど明確に区別しなくなっているということです。作曲する際にはそれらが融合し、一つの全体的なものとして響くようになっています。

もう一つは、特定のグループのために曲を書く際、常に具体的なミュージシャンの音を思い浮かべ、彼らが組み合わさったときにどんな化学反応が起きるかを想像し、聴こえてくる音を楽譜に書き起こすようにしてきました。そうすることで、プロセスは非常に有機的でシンプルなものになります。

どのようなサウンドになるかのイメージが湧き始めると、過去に別のグループで作った楽曲が可能性として浮かんでくることがあり、その場合は過去の曲を編曲したり、新しいセクションやパートを書き加えたりします。私自身、長年にわたってこの方向性に向かって取り組んできたため、このグループでもそうしたプロセスが頻繁に起きました。過去の楽曲の中に、道を示してくれる「設計図」が見えたのです。

── RU’YAにはガリア・ベナリが参加しています。彼女はこれまでのキャリアを通じて、詩を自分の音楽に取り入れてきました。彼女の存在が、このプロジェクトにもう一つの次元を加えているように感じます。彼女とは、どのようにして知り合ったのでしょうか。

私にとって最大の未知数だったのは、ガリアと一緒に仕事をすること、そしてアラビア語の詩を扱うことでした。完全に初めてというわけではありませんでしたが、決して十分に慣れていたわけでもありません。こういった意味で何かに居心地の悪さを感じるときは、たいてい、それこそが自分の進むべき方向であることが多いのです。

私たちはゲント（Ghent）で出会いました。私がHA Concertsでクリスチャンとデュオ・コンサートをやったときのことです。すぐに意気投合して、そこでバンド名を考えました。それがきっかけになってどんどん話が広がり、とても居心地のいい制作環境が生まれていったんです。彼女は素晴らしいミュージシャンで、とても直感的で冒険心がある。それが私自身のスタイルと本当によく合います。彼女は作品の中でもっとも難しいセクション、つまりアトーナル（無調）な領域に入っていくような部分でも歌ってくれました。伝統音楽にこれほど深く根ざしたアーティストにそんなことを期待していたわけではなかったので、本当に刺激的でした。

また、彼女はアラブの詩の専門家でもあり、引き出しとなる作品を豊富に持っているため、詩と書かれた楽譜が見事に調和しました。彼女の存在がプロジェクトにさらなる次元を加えていることは間違いありません。彼女は多岐にわたる分野や環境で活動しており、非常にインスピレーションを与えてくれる存在ですが、その創造性の中でもこのグループは特別な位置を占めています。

私たちのバンドには、まだ成長していく余地がたくさんあります。このプロジェクトには、まだ録音されていないもの、いや、まだライヴで演奏さえしていない要素もたくさんあるのです。メンバー全員が地理的に離れた場所に住んでいるため発展していくのに時間がかかっていますが、私たちはみんなこのプロジェクトに取り組み続ける意思を持っていますし、一緒に集まるたびに多くの新しい情報が付け加えられていくでしょう。

── メールスで観た時にガリア・べナリが朗読した詩は、パレスチナの詩人 ナセル・ラバ（Nasser Rabah）の詩でしょうか？（MCを上手く聞き取れなかったので確認です）。カナダやヨーロッパではナセル・ラバはよく知られているのでしょうか。（マフムード・ダルウィーシュの日本語訳詩集は出版されていますが、ナセル・ラバは知られていないので。）

その詩はナセル・ラバの『Kayfa Ousamehoni（どのようにして自分を許せばいいのか）』という作品です。あの曲こそが、まさにこのバンドの始まりとなりました。ハミンが私に内緒で、彼女に私たちの「Gaza」という曲を聴かせていたのです。ハミンは私に「『Gaza』という曲があるのだから、ガリアに聴かせない手はないよ」と。

彼女はその曲に即座に反応しました。以前録音していたナセルの詩に基づく曲が、私たちの曲に文字通りぴったりと重なったのです。彼女はその二つを組み合わせて私に送ってくれました。私たちは瞬く間に最初の一曲を手に入れたんです。

それ以前、私は彼の詩を知りませんでした。現在、ガリアは彼と友人ですが、もともとは共通の友人がいて、ガリアがその友人を通じて、自分がこの作品を歌っているバージョンをナセルに送りました。彼から返事が来て、「今、私たちの頭上に爆弾が落とされている。もし朝まで生きていたら、それを聴くよ」とありました。彼はその攻撃を生き延び、そして音楽を聴いて「あの日、自分に何か良いことが起こったことが嬉しい」と言ってくれました。それ以来、二人は友人になったのです。

彼の詩が、カナダや日本でももっと知られるようになればいいと思っています。日本語訳はありませんが、フランス語とヘブライ語の翻訳はあります。彼の作品の英訳はこちらから出版されています。
https://citylights.com/general-poetry/gaza-the-poem-said-its-piece-pp-64/

── ガリア・ベナリはアラビア語で歌い、詩を朗読します。詩と音楽についてどのようにお考えでしょうか。

アイデアの伝達というのは、常にいくつものレベルで起こるものだと思います。私はいつも、まず音楽を聴きます。ポップ・ソングでさえ、何度か通して聴くまでは歌詞をほとんど聴いていません。平均的な音楽リスナーにとっては、これはおそらく普通のことではないと思います。言葉のほうが最も認識しやすいものなので、それも当然でしょう。私は普段、歌詞を覚えたり細かく分析したりすることなく、そこに込められたアイデアやコンセプト、感情的なメッセージを感じ取ります。もちろん、そのせいで歌詞が意図していたことを間違って理解してしまうこともあります。でも、ときには自分自身の解釈のほうが、作者の意図よりも自分にとって意味のあるものになることもあります。

本当に詩的な文章であれば、当然、さまざまな理解や解釈が生まれやすくなります。そして、スポークン・ワードの背景として音楽があるとき、私はそれをよりはっきりと感じます。このプロジェクトでは、私はアラビア語を理解していないので、その瞬間に歌詞が意図している意味を理解しているわけではありません。でも、そこにある感情的な意図と音楽的な意図は受け取っています。ガリアは作品を深く理解していて、その中に重層的に込められた意味を説明することにも長けています。それに翻訳が加わることで、音楽により大きな深みと重み、そして理解がもたらされるのです。

音楽は感情を伝えます。それは必ずしも具体的なものではありませんが、とても重要なものです。この世界には、表現する必要があっても、それが具体的ではなく、言葉にすることさえできず、認知的に理解することすらできないものが、あまりにもたくさんあります。詩は、具体的でありながら、同時にそうした抽象性を指し示すことができます。だからこそ、詩と音楽はどちらも、人間が表現するための不可欠な手段なのでしょう。もちろん、フレージングやカデンツ、リズム、メロディなどによる自然なつながりもありますが、私にとってより刺激的なのは、こうした「儚く捉えがたいものの表現」が持つ、より深い共通性なのです。

── RU’YAを通して、私は現在進行しているパレスチナでのジェノサイドに対する抵抗の意志とともに、世界各地で起こっている紛争、また多文化共生に失敗し、完全に混乱してしまった現代社会に向けたメッセージを感じました。このプロジェクトは、ミュージシャンやアーティストが自らの作品を通して政治的な関わり方、その一つの例を示しているように感じます。

これを聞いて、偉大な詩人イェフダ・アミハイが、かつて東京での講演で語った言葉を思い出しました。質疑応答の時にアイルランド人からの質問に答えて、彼はこう言いました。

いわゆる政治的にコミットした詩、社会的に関与した詩と、そうでない詩を、私は区別しません。すべての詩は政治的です。詩を書くために象牙の塔へ逃げ込んだとしても、それもまた政治的な表明です。それは『私は関心がない』と言っていることになる。そして、関心を持たないこともまた政治的なのです。

政治と音楽の関係について、そしてミュージシャン、アーティストとしてのあなたにとって「政治的にコミットする」とはどういうことなのか、ご自身の考えを聞かせてください。

即興音楽においては、個々の人間が自分自身を表現し、時には互いに衝突しながらも、それぞれの創造や成果を尊重し祝福するための余地が残されています。誰もが、自分自身を超えた大きな何かの一部になることを目指しています。そこには妥協はありますが、個人の表現やアイデンティティを妨げるようなものではありません。そこには、ギブ・アンド・テイク、相互性、尊敬、そして敬意があります。この概念こそが、音楽的にも、個人としても、詩的にもRU’YAの中心にあります。この作品自体が、非常に強力でポジティブな政治的メッセージとなっているのです。

社会においてこれが崩れてしまうのは、自分たち自身の権力や経済的利益のために、私たちの恐怖や、「声を聞いてもらいたい」「自分を表現したい」「好奇心を育てたい」「互いから学びたい」という根本的な欲求を操り、支配しようとする力が存在するからだと思います。

もっと一般的なレベルで言えば、私はあらゆる芸術表現は政治的だと感じています。なぜなら、たとえ象牙の塔に逃げ込んで詩を書く人であっても、少なくとも個人的な芸術表現や創造について何かに時間を費やすことを選んでいるからです。資本主義が「重要なものはすべて価格（値段）がつけられなければならない」と宣言している時代に、それを行うこと自体が政治的なのです。それは、芸術が人間であることの重要な一部だと表明することです。人生は、利益に貢献するものだけで成り立っているのではない。メンタル・ヘルス、未知なるものとのつながり、自分自身のより深い部分とのつながり、そして人間性とのつながりを見つけるための重要な手段も、人生には必要なのです。

そういう意味では、真摯に芸術に取り組むアーティストは、それぞれがいわば自分自身の「ミューズ」に従っているのであり、最も誠実な作品を生み出すために、どこまで公然と政治的な姿勢を示すのかを決めるのは本人次第です。自分が何者であるかは、隠そうとしても、あるいはそれに向き合って進もうとしても、良くも悪くも、結局は自分の芸術の中に現れてくるのだと思います。もちろん、これは知的で抽象的な思考のプロセスであり、そこには美しさがあります。私が愛する芸術の多くが、こうした知的な領域で語られていることも分かっています。しかし、私自身が本当に心を動かされる偉大な芸術の多くは、もっと深遠で原初的な場所から生まれているのだと思います。それは誠実なものであると同時に、時に知的かつ抽象的な議論を内包するものでもあります。

とはいえ、二重表現（ダブルスピーク）が現実を曖昧にし、黙らせ、混同させるために使われている今、罪のない人々や子どもたちが大量に殺され、強制的な追放が行われ、政府が社会の一方の集団の優越と、もう一方の集団の従属を公言し、さらに、声を上げる人々から職業上、政治上、そして個人的な安全さえも奪われている。そういう状況において、抑圧する側をなだめるための言葉遣いについて、実りのない議論に埋没している場合ではありません。個人として、どちらの側に立つのかを明確にする責任があります。なぜなら立場を明らかにしないということは、抑圧する側の立場を取ることになるからです。権力を持つ者たちは、あなたの承認を得る必要はありません。ただ、物事を曖昧にしてしまえばいいのですから。

悲しいことに、私は今こうして話しているのが歴史上のどの時代のことでもあるように思えてしまいます。そして現在について言えば、多少の違いはあれ、スーダン、シリア北部、コンゴなどについても同じことが言えるでしょう。

それぞれの紛争の内部で何が起きているのか、その複雑な構造や文脈、歴史的な意味、そしてそこにある感情を、深く研究し、省察することなしに本当に理解することは誰にもできません。しかし、ガザとパレスチナにおける違法な入植地の問題は、私がここまで述べてきたことを明確に示す例です。

苦しみや戦争、ジェノサイドといった現実を目の当たりにした際、私たちはそれらと実際に向き合うことを避けるために、事象を理屈で捉えたり抽象化したりして、心のどこかに押し込めようとする防衛本能を働かせます。それは時に、私たちが日常生活を続け、自分たちの身近な範囲で善い行いをするためになされることでもあります。しかし、このジェノサイドを単なる理屈や概念として処理する段階は、とうの昔に終わりました。ジェノサイドは終わらせなければなりません。抑圧者に対し、世界的な抵抗を起こす必要があるのです。

Moers Festival 
May 25,2026

 
Gordon Grdina
日本を訪れて

── 話が変わりますが、あなたは2019年と2024年の2度来日し、日本のミュージシャンと共演されていますね。彼らと出会った最初のきっかけは何だったのでしょうか？

最初に道場（八木美知依、本田珠也）と巻上公一に出会ったのは、ヴロツワフで行われたJazztopad（ピョートル・トルキエヴィチがキュレーションを務めたもう一つのフェスティバル）でした。それぞれの存在は知っていましたが、直接会ったこともライブを見たこともありませんでした。彼らの音楽を個別に聴いても、一緒に演奏しているのを聴いても素晴らしいと感じ、「絶対に共演したい」と思いました。それが日本との最初の繋がりです。

マーク・ラパポートがいくつかのコンサートと録音のセッティングを手伝ってくれ、アルバムを制作することができました。私たちはGOK Soundスタジオに入り、巻上とのデュオ、八木美知依・本田珠也とのトリオ、そしてカルテットで3時間以上の音楽を録音しました。それは驚くべき体験であり、アーティストとしての彼ら一人ひとりのユニークな表現に圧倒されました。その後、私はその音源をミックス・編集して約70分の長編作品にまとめ、それがアルバムとなりました（『Gordon Grdina’s The Twain feat. Dōjō and Kōichi Makigami』）。冒頭とエンディングがアナログ盤に収録されており、全編はデジタルで聴くことができます。（→Bandcamp）

それから、武石聡とのカルテットもあります。彼は長年ニューヨークに住んでいますが、毎年数ヶ月間は日本で過ごしています。実際に日本で会ったことはないのですが、彼は非常にパワフルなミュージシャンであり素晴らしい人物で、彼と話す中で日本の音楽コミュニティについて多くを学びました。

── 私が見た公演の中では、JAZZ ART せんがわでの道場（八木美知依＋本田珠也）と巻上公一との共演が特に印象的でした。日本で共演したミュージシャンの中で、特に強い印象を残した方はいますか。

それ（グルディナ＋道場＋巻上）は、The Twainという名前の非常に多様性に富んだインパクトのあるグループです。メンバーの一人ひとりが自身の音楽的な系譜におけるマスターでありながら、そこを大きく超えて独自のサウンド世界を創造しています。私たちが集まると、共有された歴史や理解と、多くの神秘や未知が混ざり合い、音楽的に瞬時に引き込まれ、深く繋がることができるのです。あの公演と公演の間は全く演奏していなかったのですが、JAZZ ART せんがわでのステージでは、最初の1音目からあたかも何年も一緒に演奏してきたかのように音楽が展開していきました。強力な個性を持ったメンバーによるグループで、近いうちにまた共演できることを願っています。

同じ訪日期間中（2024年）、藤井郷子、田村夏樹、井谷享志、須川崇志、太田惠資といった素晴らしいミュージシャンたちとも演奏することができました。また、大友良英や灰野敬二とはデュオで共演しました。どの体験も、それぞれ私にとって深い意味を持つものでした。これらのセッションのいくつかは録音できたので、近いうちに音源としてリリースしたいと考えています。

── 音楽的、個人的、それ以外のことでもいいのですが、2度の来日で得られたものがあればお話しいただけませんか。

訪問した時間は、個人としても、音楽的にも、文化的にも非常に深い体験となりました。私自身の歴史に結びついた極めて儚い（感覚的な）ものもあれば、これほど多くの人々が密接に暮らすための優れた方法についてのアイデアなど、非常に実践的で論理的なものもありました。カナダでの経験とは大きく異なるものでしたが、バンクーバーでは日本の影響を強く感じることがあるため、共通点を感じる部分もありました。最初の旅の後、絶対にまた戻ってくると確信し、もっと頻繁に訪れる方法を模索してきました。まだ東京と横浜しか探索していないので、やりたいことがたくさんあります。

音楽的にはまだ表面をなぞった程度に過ぎませんが、すでに世界レベルのプレイヤーたちが活動する多様なシーンに対し、深い敬意と称賛の念を抱いています。私の経験した範囲では、音楽への真摯な姿勢や献身的な取り組みには、大いに刺激を受けていました。ジャズや実験的なアヴァンギャルドのコミュニティには素晴らしい歴史があり、私はそれを理解し始めたばかりです。その最初のきっかけは菊地雅章でした。彼はアーティストとして「自分に誠実であること」の意味を体現する、実に素晴らしい道標のような存在です。彼に直接お会いする機会はありませんでしたが、会ってみたかったですね。

今後、このような卓越したミュージシャンたちのコミュニティを、もっと本格的に探求できる機会が得られればと思っています。個人的には、家族も連れて日本全国をツアーで回ってみたいと思っています。それから、最近サーフィンも始めたので、沖縄を訪れて、この国の自然の美しさをもっと発見したいです。

JAZZ ART Sengawa  
January 13,2024

items._cn_summary: 加拿大乌德/吉他演奏家戈登·格鲁迪纳发起跨国项目RU'YA，汇聚突尼斯、土耳其、奥地利、伊朗、德国等不同国籍与文化背景的乐手，将阿拉伯马卡姆、波斯音乐、即兴演奏与当代爵士语汇融为一体。乐队核心由格鲁迪纳、歌手加利亚·贝纳利、钢琴/合成器手伊利亚斯·施特梅塞德、打击乐手哈敏·霍纳里与鼓手克里斯蒂安·利林格组成，编制强调人声、诗歌与器乐即兴的交织。演出中朗诵巴勒斯坦诗人纳塞尔·拉巴的诗作，赋予项目鲜明的政治立场与文化批判维度。作品编排兼顾严谨作曲框架与高度自由的即兴空间，跨文化音色对话层次丰富，既具学院派当代音乐的精密结构，又保留世界音乐传统的开放呼吸。

items.body: After several records examining language (Pause/Stutter/Uh/Repeat), mutation (Mutate), liturgical memory (Ison), and the algorithmic logic of social media (Kitbashing), Abadir arrives at what feels like the conceptual centre of his work. The Primitivist is not simply a new collection of club tracks but a declaration of intent, rejecting electronic music’s enduring fixation with futurism in favour of a deeper engagement with the present and with the musical traditions that continue to shape it. The title is deliberately provocative. As Abadir has argued in an article for Cartography of Darkness, electronic music has spent decades equating novelty with the future, often reproducing the same cyberpunk imagery, dystopian fantasies and technological narratives inherited from the 1980s and 1990s. For him, that obsession has become a form of nostalgia masquerading as progress, one increasingly detached from the realities of communities living through war, authoritarianism and displacement. The Primitivist proposes another direction altogether: creativity rooted not in speculative futures but in sustained engagement with living musical heritage and the political urgency of the present. That shift is immediately audible. If Mutate revolved around the Egyptian maqsoum rhythm, this EP opens its vocabulary to rhythmic traditions and performance practices from across the Arab world. The opening “Habban” takes its name from the Gulf bagpipe, a celebratory folk instrument associated with communal dancing and percussion ensembles. Rather than sampling tradition as an exotic signifier, Abadir absorbs its rhythmic logic into a contemporary club framework where darbuka, khishba, mijwiz and intricate hand-clapping patterns become structural rather than decorative elements. The ecstatic propulsion of “The Primitivist” and the playful destabilisation of “Pass & Go” continue that trajectory, while the closing “This Is Not Another Maqsoum” knowingly acknowledges — and moves beyond — the rhythmic strategy that defined his previous album. What remains constant throughout Abadir’s catalogue is his concern with transformation. Each record asks a different question, yet all are linked by the same compositional impulse: taking existing sonic materials — speech, liturgy, social media, club music or regional traditions — and discovering how they can be reimagined without losing their historical or cultural specificity. The result is music that consistently resists easy categorisation. It is uncompromisingly contemporary, yet never relies on futurist rhetoric to justify its newness. In an electronic music landscape still eager to describe unfamiliar sounds as “futuristic,” The Primitivist offers a persuasive alternative. It suggests that innovation need not emerge from imagined worlds or technological fantasies. Sometimes it begins by listening more closely to the present and to histories that have always been there, waiting to be heard. photo by Omar Elkafrawy To helps us see beyond the future, we reached out directly to Abadir. The Primitivist presents itself as a rejection of electronic music’s long-standing fascination with futurism. You’ve argued that futurist narratives often reflect Eurocentric ideas of progress while overlooking the lived realities of communities experiencing war or authoritarianism. Once you reject futurism as the dominant framework, what new possibilities does “primitivism” open up for composition? Does it change the way you think about rhythm, sound design or even the social function of club music? My rejection of anything related to futurism has been going for five years, and each year it becomes more radical. I think this makes sense to me at the moment, since the future, futurism and the futuristic have been the main focus in electronic music since the 80’s (if not even before that) to identify what’s new, what’s next and the unheard for the western ears. This narrative of futurism has been already ruling for 40 years, which makes it outdated for me and repetitive to the maximum, to the point where it’s now reduced to a marketing label. It became a habit to link newness to the future, and unfortunately there has been a lack of critique to this idea, or attempts to link creativity and newness to something else other than futurism. It’s even nostalgic that futurism in electronic music is still somehow based on the same concepts, sounds and perspectives that once existed in the 80’s or the 90’s. There have been cycles of criticizing Mark Fisher’s theories, with a general claim that the future didn’t stop and “gotcha Fisher you are wrong”, because X or Y (from the global north) made “futuristic” music. Honestly, this argument is haunted by an outdated vision of what futuristic music means, it’s also haunted by the urge of futurism. That’s nostalgia for futurism (which is different from Fisher’s concept of lost futures) that used to exist decades ago. It’s paradoxical, and in that sense futurism is eating itself. But I think this sort of discussion doesn’t fit the Arabic context because we have different realities and priorities. With the exception of Afrofuturism, the futuristic narrative is escapist and out of touch with the present. It chooses progress and speed rather than understanding and facing the present. The narrative for years has been about fetishising dystopia or the other opposite, techno-optimism led by the “punchline” of “Let’s imagine a future where…” I see both narratives out of touch with reality, especially now. Being able to think like that is a kind of luxury, rather than living the hard present reality which is unfolding in front of our eyes on a daily basis. So at least, an action must be taken to change that, and actions happen in the present. Once we reach a point where present issues are kind of fixed, then we can have the time and luxury to speculate, think about the future and imagine it. More thoughts about this topic can be found in this essay I wrote last year. I chose the term Primitivism as a provocation, a way to say I’m happy I’m not futuristic, I’m busy with the present and I’m inspired by a deeply rooted music heritage. This way of thinking is definitely inspiring because making this claim means that I need to listen, revisit, read and learn a lot about music from the Arab region on the technical, cultural and historical level. During the last few years I learned a lot about Maqamat, rhythms from different parts of the Arab region. As you said, this also had an impact on sound design, because you can easily tell that the sound design in The Primitivist and my coming project is different from what’s in Kitbashing and Ison. On Mutate, the maqsoum rhythm acted almost as the album’s organising principle, whereas The Primitivist draws from a much broader range of rhythmic traditions and instrumental references from Iraq, Kuwait, Syria and Palestine. Tracks such as “Habban”, “The Primitivist” and “This Is Not Another Maqsoum” feel less concerned with hybridising genres than with rethinking the vocabulary of club music itself. How did your compositional approach change between these two records, and did moving beyond maqsoum also change the way you thought about rhythm? Usually I tend to link my projects together, as well as old and fresh ideas. What starts as a sound or an idea in one project will be revisited and developed more a few years later. You can trace that between Pause/Stutter/Uh/Repeat and Kitbashing or Ison, and between Mutate and The Primitivist. This marks the continuity of my work. Maqsoum was the center of Mutate, next to the influence of other club genres that I listen to and DJ. I wasn’t making club music before Mutate, so it made sense to me to start with a sound I’m familiar with and stuck in my memory, which is Maqsoum. It was fun mixing Jungle and Footwork or Jersey with sped up and cut up Maqsoum samples, to come up with a mutated club sound. In The Primitivist I decided to focus more on Arabic rhythms and dropping the influences of other club genres. During a 3 year period I got attracted to sounds from the countries you mentioned and I extended my knowledge to further other rhythmic patterns. The result was working with rhythmic sounds related to Dahhiya, Dabke, simulating a real drummer playing the Khishba or using the Sharbaka, which is a hand clapping technique rooted in the Arabian Gulf, especially in Kuwait. In my coming project, I’m going deeper in sound design, and more complex patterns with a focus on variations in time signatures. There is a striking tension throughout the EP between recognisable Arab instruments—mijwiz pipes, darbuka, khishba, brass timbres—and an approach to rhythm and sound design that remains uncompromisingly contemporary. As someone who has also been exploring Arabic maqamat and instrumental playing techniques in your more recent work, how do you avoid turning these traditions into cultural signifiers or markers of authenticity, allowing them instead to remain living musical materials? I think the idea is about avoiding orientalist and self-orientalist cliches, or lazy fusion, in addition to finding this common ground between the familiar and the unfamiliar, with surprise elements. Once you hear a Mijwiz or a brass synth for instance, you will get that sense of “yes I know that”, then twisting the expectations is the next crucial step. If I hear a Rast or Huzam or Bayati maqam used by an Arabic producer, I will see it as normal. But creativity appears depending on some other factors such as: the articulation and ornamentation in maqamat, the modulation between maqamat, how the producer is implementing these maqamat with drum patterns, how the sound design is made, how the arrangement is done and the structure is built. Here you have a lot of options to twist the expectations. Yet, I still admire the musicians who are maintaining old traditions as they are, because we need that now in our region more than any time before, given the external threat by the infamous pariah state, liberal capitalist “values”, A.I, the Dubaification of our region. This is the very material reality we face and we have to deal with in the present, so again, what future exactly are we talking about? Koleyet El Banat – photo by Omar Elkafrawy Your work sits at an unusual intersection of artistic practice and critical writing. As the editor of the electronic music section at Ma3azef, you’re constantly analysing how electronic music is written about, categorised and historicised. Has writing criticism changed the way you make music? Conversely, has producing records like The Primitivist made you more critical of the vocabulary and frameworks through which electronic music — particularly music from the Arab world — is discussed in western publications? My criticism towards the vocabulary and frameworks used in western publications as well as the westernised Arabic ones has always been there. I also believe that the music journalist or the critic has to read, follow and listen a lot, a good level of curiosity is required. I’m trying to do my best with that, so my critique can have some basis. Maybe The Primitivist is a result of that. It’s about how to express critique through a medium other than writing; proposing that we don’t need to be obsessed with the future or futurism to be creative, alternatively, we can be focused in the present or we can draw inspiration from our cultural roots. The present is here already. The same applies on Kitbashing by the way, one can theorise about its concept in an essay or a book, but I wanted to represent the concept sonically. Definitely, working in criticism has made me think differently about my own music, because it has made me much more self-critical. My music projects are slow cooked, and each one starts with a simple question: why am I doing this or what am I trying to say? This question can be frustrating or provocative to some artists, but for me it makes total sense and it’s the main critical question behind every project.ِ During the process, I can be very critical and harsh towards myself, but it helps me a lot. With Kitbashing, you proposed feeding on the algorithm rather than feeding it, transforming the sounds of social media into compositional material. In retrospect, do you think the algorithm can ever truly be subverted, or does every attempt at resisting it inevitably become another form of participation? On an individual level, we can benefit from the algorithm, whether by using it for learning purposes, an introduction to something, being informed about cultural or political topics, or simply watching something fun, because we need a break. Apart from that, ِI wish in general that the algorithm is subverted for something good and I think this has to be collectively done. Take for instance the non-commercial electronic music scene which is now driven by the algorithmic scrolling mentality, everyone from the curators, to the spaces, to the artists, to the press, to the crowd, is so invested in an app. Everything has been highly dependent on Instagram. It has become the main way to be heard and seen and that’s exhausting and frustrating. A couple of slides or a polished one minute video from the peak of a live or DJ set defines an artist. But imagine that the press and curators are relatively withdrawing from Instagram, this can have a good impact on producers and DJs, they will spend less time on the app, and post less, only when it’s necessary. This will make the crowd spend more time listening and reading, and artists will only focus on their music and their work. That would be ideal, isn’t it? (Gianmarco Del Re)

items._cn_summary: Abadir延续其系列探索，将阿拉伯世界多元节奏传统——海湾风笛、达布卡鼓、米吉威兹管与手掌击拍——融入当代俱乐部框架，替代电子乐对未来的执念。专辑并非简单采样民俗符号，而是将这些乐器的节奏逻辑转化为结构骨架，使传统成为创作方法论而非异域装饰。从埃及马克苏姆节奏到泛阿拉伯节奏语汇的拓展，以及终曲对前作策略的自觉超越，体现出持续的概念演化。音乐拒绝以未来主义修辞为新意辩护，转而主张深度聆听当下与活态传统。在战争与流离的现实语境下，这种扎根于地方历史的创作取向本身即具有政治意味。整体呈现出拒绝被轻易归类的杂糅美学，在俱乐部节奏与文化记忆之间建立了有张力的对话。

items.body:
Curating a retrospective of 40 years of recorded music is a daunting task, particularly when it is your own. Accurately representing the arc of the work and the life that created it requires frankness and acceptance. It is a process punctuated with winces and sighs and the occasional grin. Composer and improviser Jin Hi Kim experienced it all when compiling The Jin Hi Kim Collection, recently issued by Neuma. If the use of “odyssey” requires a great voyage, discovering new lands, and encountering titans, then Kim’s journey easily qualifies. Not only did she leave Korea at 23 for the US in 1980, Kim traversed an arguably greater gulf by leaving her elite training in traditional Korean music to study electronic music and composition with Lou Harrison, Terry Riley, and others. In the intervening decades, she worked with leading exponents of contemporary composition and improvisation like Kronos Quartet and Derek Bailey, and transformed the komungo, the traditional five-foot-long lute dating from the 4th Century CE, exponentially extending its sonic range through computer interfaces and signal processing.

Rediscovery accompanied the selection process for the 9-CD Collection. She was especially surprised when reviewing early works transliterating Korean music through Western instruments, or employing graphic notation. “It was created by a young mind,” Kim recently recalled with a laugh. “Sometimes it was hard to hear that’s what I did. But it was also good evidence for an archival collection. It was a wonderful feeling to look at everything I did – well, almost everything – but one thing that I was really proud about it is that there is not just one kind of music. Each piece has its Korean roots but, like I’ve said, I came to America to make new music, so I look at my 40 years of work and, yeah, I achieved that. So, it was a very satisfying process.

“When I listen to some of the improvisations, I realized how young and unafraid I was. Komungo has a limited sound compared to other instruments. When you work with virtuoso improvisers, they have vocabularies that are so rich. They are creating so many different colors and textures, but komungo has limits. It doesn’t allow you to express so much of the story. It has a meditative energy, of nothingness, of slowness. I was so brave to use this instrument with such incredible masters and to communicate with them and create music with them. I did it somehow with my inner energy. I was able to present this inner energy.”

The Collection almost equally divides Kim’s work in composition and improvisation, with five discs devoted to works for orchestra and chamber music ensembles, and four documenting improvisations with, among others, an impressive diversity of percussionists, including Gerry Hemingway, Susie Ibarra, and Tony Oxley, and string players like Bill Frisell, Min Xiao-Fen, and Hans Reichel. If anything can be read into it, the slight tilt reflects her ardent pursuit to articulate the concept of Living Tones Compositions, and how central it is to her work.

“The most important thing about the Living Tones Compositions is to convey the Korean element and philosophy through Western contemporary music,” she explained. “When I came to the United States after training in traditional Korean music, European classical music was more respected in Korea than the traditional music. They didn’t know much about American avant-garde music then, in the 1970s. I was a young musician who trained with the very best teachers and saw that I was not respected because I was not doing Western music.

“That created within me a great desire to fix that problem. You can’t fix anything, but I was young, I had a passion and a mission. I was living in the United States; I was composing for Western musicians; so how could I make this Korean idea, this Korean state of mind in making music, how could I put this together with Western music with equal respect? That was my thing. All my Living Tones Compositions come from the idea of putting together the Korean context and philosophy and Western instruments and musical context, to see how Western musicians took to the Korean attitude – not necessarily techniques, scales, anything like that – but this attitude, this state of mind. That’s what I’m doing with Living Tones music.

“Korean traditional music was once influenced by Chinese music,” Kim prefaced to explain the context and philosophy of Korean music, which she also detailed extensively in her book, Duality of Ancient Korean Roots and Western New Music. “Korean music can be divided into folk music and court music. Court music was quite different from music of ordinary people. The court was deeply influenced by ancient Chinese philosophy – yin and yang; the five elements, and ancient ancestors worship. The music wasn’t entertainment; it was ritual – that was part of both court and folk music. For ordinary people, they associated music with the shaman. For court music, there were virtuoso musicians who created an austere music, based on a philosophy of cosmic sound and abstract thinking; but for ordinary people, the shaman always took care of pain, community pain. Music was performed for celebrations of harvests and other things, but more for problems like drought, someone who is sick, some kind of problem. The shaman is always dealing with the problem of pain in their lives. They always had to sing something very sad. Her song has nothing to do with joyous things – always grief and pain. Ordinary people related to that.

“Both court and folk music had an emphasis on energy – they never thought of music as just sound. It had healing energy. In the folk community, they tried to imitate the shaman, the way she sang, shaking the notes, trying to reach out to another spirit, trying to connect heaven and earth. If you listen to a shaman’s song, there’s a very strong vibrato. The instrumentalists who don’t sing listen to this type of music; it’s very touching, very soulful, and it reflects the problems in their lives. Korean instrumentalists are all shaking, shaking their hands, shaking their instruments, shaking their notes. I play komungo, where the strings can move a lot, up and down, so you can really shake the notes and express the music in the same way as the shaman. I translate that process, that context, that spirit, into Living Tones. Each tone has its own light, and because it has its own light, its time is elastic. It is not like abstract Western time, where you count the time of each note perfectly, and you don’t have the space for microtones. There’s no time to do that in Western music. Time becomes much more open and that’s why in Korean music they don’t talk about abstract time but time in a cycle. Within that cycle, you have a lot of freedom of how to use that space with deep vibratos or any other articulation to create that intense feeling.”

The qualities Kim ascribes to Korean music are manifest in the komungo. It has a palpably plangent sound, with a bass register lower and more resonant than the guembri’s and the sting of ancient harps in its highest notes. It has a timbral luster comparable to the dark, iridescent glazes of pit-fired ceramics or the blocks of deep color that hover over the black basecoats of a Mark Rothko painting. Its dredge-like twang and the skeletal figures central to the music stop the racing, associative Western mind dead in its tracks. Even before Kim augmented the instrument with signal processing, Western improvisers had a strong attraction to the komungo. Conversely, improvisation has, over the decades, impacted Kim’s outlook.

However, Kim has a nuanced view on how improvisation has influenced her. “Influence is the result over a long period,” she elaborated, “because I played with a person one time or two times. That long period is a really deep space. It’s not that a particular musician gave me something. It is that the experience of playing with someone becomes part of my life experience. Now I look at something differently than when I was young. I understand how the universe works because of scientists and I understand how improvisation works because of improvisers. When you travel all around the world – I’ve performed in over 60 countries and have lived in some of these countries for a long time, six months or even a year – then you have an incredibly different life perspective. All of those things interest me. So, I have been influenced by many things over the decades, so that when I play with someone, it is not just that moment I am responding to; it’s everything about the other musicians: their instruments; their traditions; their culture. That gives me a very clear idea what to do.

“When I was young, I was so desperate to communicate successfully with each improviser I played with. I was trying to understand their personality; I was trying to understand their vocabulary. There have been very few times that I played on the spot without any information about the people I was playing with. I had heard them before I had the opportunity to play with them, playing with other musicians or solo. In my own way, I understood who they are. If I don’t understand them and their musical elements, I have no way to contribute anything on komungo. I have to understand their personality, their energy, how they process the music. Not all people process the same way; some people are poetic; some people are very emotional; some people are very funny. Everybody has those things happening. Understanding that was very important to me. It helped me to communicate, to hear what they were giving me, so I could give back. I listened a lot to what they were doing at a particular moment.”

Given that improvisers spanning James Newton and Elliott Sharp, and Rüdiger Carl and Oliver Lake, are heard throughout the box set, it is noteworthy that Kim singles one out to illustrate her approach to improvisation. “When I work with William Parker, he has a very deep energy in his soul,” she said of the bassist. “When I played with him, he influenced me with his deep energy. It’s really big. That influenced me to be really big. That bigness, that abundance, that tireless energy; that lets us play a really long time. He has the qualities to do something that a Korean shaman could do, playing the same idea over and over and over for a long time – trance like – but the energy becomes more powerful. William Parker has that type of energy. The bass is like the komungo; it has a deep energy and incredible power. I’m really influenced by that.”

Retrospectives like the Collection are generally considered to be merely summations, but in Kim’s case, it is more a marker of distance travelled and journeys ahead. “It reflects my continuous evolution as an artist. Throughout my musical journey, I have always searched for new ways to express myself creatively while remaining deeply rooted in my Korean musical identity.

“In essence, every work in this collection is the result of my enduring desire to elevate often-neglected Korean aesthetics, shaped alongside the freedom I found in America – a place that allowed me to pursue my artistic passions and ideas without limitation.

“Today, my perspective extends beyond national boundaries to the increasingly interconnected global community. I have aspired to use music as a spiritual and transformative force to confront social challenges. I believe this has become the new direction of my artistic journey.”

Kim’s new direction has steered her towards to uplifting marginalized subalterns and breaking through the fourth wall of the concert hall separating musicians from listeners. “Right now, because the world has changed so much, and America is now so blue, and so many people are mentally ill – I know because I recently gave a music meditation workshop at the Yale mental health center – I want to do something about community pain. I always go back to what the shaman does. I think I have sort of achieved my goal of blending Korean and Western ways of thinking with Living Tones, so right now I want to make music that the community participates in. Not necessarily well-trained musicians, but anybody who is interested. I already started on this in 2023 with a piece called ‘Ritual for Earth.’ I would like to do these things for now. I’m not anxious about my career or my next commission. I’m thinking about community pain, environmental issues like wildfires and floods, the world we are living in. So, if I have the opportunity, working with communities is what I want to do.”

items._cn_summary: 这张九碟套装回顾了韩裔作曲家兼即兴演奏家Jin Hi Kim四十年的创作生涯。她从韩国传统音乐科班出身，转向电子音乐与作曲，曾与Lou Harrison、Terry Riley、Kronos Quartet、Derek Bailey等合作。专辑最大亮点在于对传统乐器玄琴的彻底改造——通过计算机接口与信号处理，将这件源自四世纪的五尺长琴扩展出前所未有的声响范围。套装五张碟收录管弦乐与室内乐作品，四张碟记录与Gerry Hemingway、Susie Ibarra、Bill Frisell等大师的即兴合作。Kim的创作始终扎根于韩国传统，却不断突破至新音乐领域，从图形记谱到跨界即兴，展现了一位艺术家在不同文化语境间持续迁徙与重塑的过程。

items.body:
CD/DVD DISKS
NO. 341
#2457 『みずのとう / 陽』
2026年9月19日
齊藤聡

Text by Akira Saito 齊藤聡

ROW project records

Yanagawa Homei 柳川芳命 (alto sax, soprano sax)
Reiko Nonoyama 野々山玲子 (drums, piano)

1. Improvisation No.9
2. Improvisation No.5
3. Improvisation No.2
4. Improvisation No.16
5. Improvisation No.7
6. Improvisation No.14

Recorded at 2014 studio, Chiryu, Aichi, Japan
May 11th, June 23th, and July 30th, 2026
Recorded, mixed, mastered by Reiko Nonoyama

みずのとう（MizunotoU）はサックスの柳川芳命とドラムスの野々山玲子のデュオユニットである。ふたりが知立のスタジオに3日間籠って吹き込んだ音が、2枚のアルバムとしてリリースされた。ひとつが本盤『陽』であり、もうひとつがデジタル限定の『陰』である。

筆者は、野々山のドラミングについては、横方向に動いてグルーヴを作り出すというよりは、縦方向に積み上げるかたちをつぎつぎに変貌させていくことに独創性があるとみる。それは静的な計画を指向するものではない。野々山が積み上げた構築物の上や横を柳川の音がかすめて飛んでゆき、その関係性に応じて次の構築物に挑むありようが伝わってくる。すなわち構築物じたいも動的な即興の実践によるものだ。

驚いたことに野々山はピアノも弾いているのだが、その動的な姿勢はドラムスと同様である。だが音の貌には愛嬌も相手を騙そうとする底意地の悪さもあって可笑しい。柳川も挑発されて笑っていたのではなかろうか。

もうひとつの大きな驚きは、柳川のサックスの音がかなり透明性を増したように思えることだ。これは音色だけの話ではない。かつて濁りも野蛮も受け容れていたアジアン・ブルースからは外連味が削ぎ落されているようであり、音を出してしまったことへの恥辱など皆無なのではないか。そのうえで野々山と挑むコミュニケーションの音である。

一期一会の即興演奏であることには間違いないが、成熟した大人の対話だということができる。

（文中敬称略）

参考　『みずのとう / 陰』

items._cn_summary: 这张专辑是萨克斯手柳川芳命与鼓手/钢琴家野々山玲子组成的双人即兴组合みずのとう在爱知县知立工作室三日密集录制的成果，与数字限定的姊妹专辑《陰》互为表里。全部六首曲目均以即兴编号命名，强调一期一会的对话性。乐评指出野々山的鼓点不构建横向律动，而是纵向堆叠、持续变形，柳川的萨克斯则在这些动态构造间穿梭飞行；后者令人意外的是钢琴演奏同样呈现动态姿态，且音色中带有狡黠与戏谑。柳川的萨克斯声音较以往更趋透明，去除了亚洲布鲁斯时期的粗粝与外连味，呈现出无掩饰的成熟对话气质。整张专辑呈现出两位成熟音乐人之间高度自省的即兴实践。

items.excerpt: Photo by Vins Pedrata. Courtesy the artist Sven Fritz is an artist from Germany, who has various ongoing projects that explore performance, experimental music, and sound art. items.body: Photo by Vins Pedrata. Courtesy the artist Sven Fritz is an artist from Germany, who has various ongoing projects that explore performance, experimental music, and sound art. We had the chance to converse over email about his latest work, Der Saal tobt, realized under the Ervin Omsk moniker, published by Orange Milk. The interview was edited collaboratively with the artist. David Murrieta Flores (ACL): Hi Sven, could you please talk a bit about the Ervin Omsk project for readers who are unfamiliar with it? Sven Fritz (EO): Hi David, sure. Ervin Omsk is a pseudonym I’ve been using to release experimental electronic music since 2020. The name doesn’t actually have any special meaning; it’s simply an anagram of my two first names. The project began in 2018 with a few musical collages that were strongly connected to the idea of exploring an abstract painting or sculpture in a particular room—in other words, a very spatial approach, in which I combined diverse sounds from a modular system, field recordings, voice, and so on. Fortunately, Orange Milk was willing to release these tracks on tape in 2020, with artwork by Keith Rankin. In 2023, a second album, titled Schmalster Point, was released on vinyl, with artwork by Brenna Murphy. Now the third album, Der Saal tobt, is being released on tape and CD, with artwork by Lukas Schmenger. Ervin Omsk is currently one of several projects I’m working on. However, it’s the only solo project, and therefore also the most intense one. All my other projects are collaborative—for example, most recently with the French musician Amédée de Murcia. Together, we released an album in March on the Italian label Søvn. There’s also the Hui project, which I’m doing together with Johannes Schebler (Baldruin). An album has just been released on Jollies, and another one was released on Nonlocal Research last year. I’m also part of the artist collective Trickster, where I collaborate with other artists to realize scenarios in the sense of a Gesamtkunstwerk. My role here often involves musical performances lasting several hours and spread out over multiple days. All of my projects fall within the realm of experimental electronic music, and Ervin Omsk really benefits from the many experiences I’ve had working with all these other musicians. This applies not only to production, but also to the concerts I play as Ervin Omsk. These performances, however, are more like interpretations or improvised versions of the tracks I release. ACL: As the liner notes describe it, Der Saal tobt is mimicry of an orchestral body. Usually, we would understand such a body as mechanically efficient and well-coordinated, tuned and built through practice. However, the album understands it differently, and the result is slightly opposite: it’s a body that seems “unpracticed”. How do you understand the relationships between these bodies’ organs? How do you understand the differences between the modern, “well-oiled” orchestra and the album’s version of it? EO: I recently went to a concert where a chamber ensemble performed a piece that really moved me. At the same time, I realized that I actually didn’t really know what was going on. I have no academic background in this field. For example, I lack knowledge of music history and theory, notation, instrumentology, the roles within an ensemble, and so on. So I can only form a vague idea of what is happening in this music. I sense its dissonance, complexity, and openness; at times, it almost feels improvised. At the same time, I associate orchestral music with something highbrow and inaccessible. And that would be, so to speak, a different perspective from the outside. I generally have a rather ambivalent relationship with high culture, because it often caters to unchanging expectations and cultivates a kind of institutional sophistication. And in this context, the terms “efficient” and “coordinated” become interesting: these are actually very performance-oriented categories, which I would spontaneously associate with economics and sport. What do they have to do with music? But yes, an orchestra also needs this high degree of functionality, because, for example, it follows an idea or an order in the form of a notation. The musicians ensure that everything runs smoothly because they have mastered their instruments. To put it bluntly, we could argue that a modern, well-oiled orchestra must function—which sounds almost a bit cold and predictable. In music or art, however, I am not interested in categories like “well rehearsed,” “efficient,” and “coordinated” at first. It is rather the state outside these functions that moves me. To me, the intuitive and the seemingly contradictory have always been special qualities. There is, for example, that brief moment when an orchestra or a small ensemble tunes up. It is an undefined jumble of sounds, a wonderful moment of uncertainty. I am fascinated by the orchestra pit and its sound. But I come from a different musical background, both technically and culturally. I only play guitar, I can sing, and I know some things about synths and computer music. So I can’t imitate the orchestra; I can only bring electronic instruments into play, which then, through practice, become their own form of an orchestral body. And the interactions between the organs aren’t without tension; they sometimes get in each other’s way, and they don’t always speak the same language. And that’s what makes their relationships so special to me. There’s no oil here—more like sand in the gears and friction, to stick with your analogy. ACL: What is the process that you follow in order to craft a track? How do you understand the connections between tracks, once they are finished? EO: I can hardly describe it, really. There is no linear or additive process: each track is the result of countless intuitive decisions, right down to the smallest moments. I’m obsessed with details. The computer of course offers infinite possibilities and an overwhelming freedom. But that also means I usually can’t remember how the individual tracks were made. But I’ll try to describe it using the last track on the album as an example—which was actually the first track I produced: Right at the beginning, I made some very simple and short recordings of an alto recorder that I had borrowed from a friend and musician. After sampling and processing these recordings, the flute’s physical qualities were still there—the airiness, the directness, the softness, the hiss, and so on—but I could tune it freely and also control its overtones and noise, among other things. In fact, it suddenly seemed more like a symbol for an entire group of woodwind instruments or like an instrument that wanted to be several at once. And yet it still had something artificial about it. This impression was reinforced by the way it was played. Arpeggiators, whose tempo and rate were modulated by LFOs; animated envelopes that made glissandos possible; and the layering of several abstract flutes at once, varying only in their playing and sound. Then combined and blended with noises and glitches that picked up on the flutes’ patterns and intonations, countered them, and made them seem alien. Then it got a bit crowded, maybe like rush hour at the main train station. So then it was a constant process of sorting, resampling, stretching, compressing, cutting, copying, pasting, deleting, and leaving pauses—until the track was finished. Something like that, very roughly. And as I said, there’s no single process that applies equally to all tracks. Other tracks have undergone several transformations. They were actually finished; then I completely rearranged them in the context of the entire album, because they didn’t feel right within the album’s dynamic, and the sequence of the tracks that unfolds over just 27 minutes. In addition, on this album I deliberately used certain sounds—such as the processed alto recorder— in several tracks, either obviously or just as a trace. And then, for me, all the pieces take place in the same space; they’re close and direct. Photo of Trickster setup by Sven Fritz. Courtesy the artist. ACL: What sort of gear do you use in this process? Thinking of gear less in terms of straightforward tools, and more socially in terms of extensions of your own thoughts and body, what does all this gear allow you to do? What does it inhibit you from doing? EO: I always try not to own too much gear. Even in production, I use only a few very specific and experimental tools so as not to unnecessarily expand the range of possibilities: a small modular system, MIDI controllers, Ableton Live, with digital samplers, sound generators, M4L devices, a few effects, and then a few flutes and microphones. I like the second part of your question. As a child, I played a home organ—two manuals, bass pedals. After that, I played electric guitar and sang for a long time, always in the context of bands. Vocals and guitar, in particular, are two very direct and physical instruments. It’s almost impossible to transfer that feeling to the world of synthesizers and computers, because playing them is less about gestures and more about fine motor skills involving the hands, fingers, eyes and ears: knobs, pads, trackpads, clicking, looking, listening and so on. But when it comes to abstract thinking about music, synthesizers and computers offer another advantage. They expand the scope of what I can imagine musically and put me in a constant state of learning and wonder. It’s sometimes like a rush. Surely also because I don’t understand everything. But in any case, it changes my own perception of sound, because these machines basically function like auditory microscopes. You can dive incredibly deep with your ears and your thoughts. ACL: Going back to the idea of orchestration, do you understand yourself as the orchestra’s director? Perhaps the orchestra itself, as an abstract embodiment? Perhaps the orchestra’s prompt-maker, to use contemporary code? In short – what is your own position within or without the orchestral body of the album? EO: A prompt-maker relies on clear codes or language as commands, right? That wouldn’t be immediate enough. And unfortunately, I don’t know much about the work of a conductor. But if I may set that aside for a moment, it might be something between a conductor and the orchestra itself. Here’s how I picture it: there’s a room full of objects, no musicians. So I rush through the ranks and set these objects into motion, sound, gestures, and relationships with one another. That would be very closely linked to experiences with live performances—both the role of the conductor and the abstract embodiment. Two examples: There’s this collective project called Trickster, which I’ve already mentioned: very irregularly, we realize a series of evenings as an image—no hierarchy, no stage, no beginning, no end, and thus no mood-setting service. In one of the those projects, I arranged 6–8 different speakers, several mixers, an electric guitar, a spontaneous choir of friends, several synthesizers, a percussionist, and two friends playing the French horn and the soprano recorder, spread throughout a room of about 100 square meters. Here, my role was more like that of a conductor who, over the course of about five hours, activated and collaged all of this using clear impulses and several loopers. Charging and discharging the space, playfully and improvisationally. Then recently I put together a live setup for some shows that had to fit into a backpack. A computer, two MIDI controllers, a small semi-modular synthesizer, and a microphone for vocals. Yet I prepared it in such a way that there were always five different instruments that I could play simultaneously. That was a bit demanding, but very direct, all on a small table—more as if I were many instruments, or, if you will, the orchestra itself. Turning knobs, playing pads, plugging in cables, tuning, singing, applying effects, controlling, not controlling. Photo by Matt Favero. Courtesy the artist. ACL: I’d like to return now to the question of mimicry – it’s an aesthetically loaded term, but it’s possible to contrast it with the idea that there is something organic to the body we are listening to in the album. If we understand the album’s body as more of an automaton, what are its possibilities/capacities/abilities when thinking about traditional musical categories of representation like “expression”? EO: Oh, that’s a really tough question, and I’m not sure I fully understand it. Mechanization could also be understood as a rigid and hierarchical process, but the automaton of the album feels alive to me. That would be more like a cyborg, right? But sure, let’s stick with the image of the automaton. I don’t think of it as a concrete thing with a particular physical form, but rather as an abstract machine, as algorithms and processes. In order to see what abilities it has in terms of traditional musical categories, I have to listen to it. So I’ll pretend for a moment that I didn’t build the automaton. At first, it sounds to me like a machine that seems to define its own form, processes, and movements, acrobatic and unpredictable, like a shapeshifter. It leads an inscrutable life of its own. The mistakes it makes are constantly incorporated into its search for form. A complex and delicate act. But only on the first, and perhaps the second, listening. Once you have become familiar with the complexity, the mechanisms, and the glitches, the form and nature of the automaton become clearer. Perhaps that is the moment when we can return to the “category of representation,” once we have understood the language of the automaton. Because “musical expression” may not be as organic, immediate, and human as we like to think. It is also part of a tradition and works through codes, conventions, expectations, and learned gestures—only seemingly self-evident. The automaton, of course, is only indirectly part of this tradition. In this logic, perhaps the ability of the automaton does not lie in “expressing” something in the classical sense, but in using, shifting, exaggerating, or also refusing these codes of expression. It maybe has the potential to transform many different sounds, instruments, gestures, figures, and experiments into a different but nevertheless familiar form of expression. And perhaps through its artificiality and distance it can make something audible that a human body would not do in this way. But the question really is very abstract. I hope I was able to give a somewhat meaningful answer here. Photo by Tobias Ullrich. Courtesy the artist. ACL: You did, thank you! Now, I’m interested in the meaning of the various track titles. There’s a playful overtone about things going wrong, failing in wholesome ways, or simply being the result of an essay in something (the “Memo Grisaille”, for instance, which alludes to the formative, practical painting made in shades of black or grey that emerged in the Renaissance). What links the process through which you made each track with the titles you chose for them? EO: Collecting titles or sentences is an independent process that I and other friends have been practicing since art school. I’m interested in titles because they add an associative layer to the individual track or the entire album. The album artwork by Lukas Schmenger does that too, by the way. Like the artwork, the titles are an important part of the album, even though they only come into the process at a later stage. I think the titles of the album relate in a certain way to its dynamics and moods. So I really associate the album title “Der Saal tobt” with an image of an agitated and unrestrained group of people. A feeling and sound somewhere between threat and excitement maybe. At the same time, it’s important for me to break up some kind of sonic overload with an everyday and blunt remark like “Beim besten Willen,” which rather expresses a refusal or incomprehension. So I also like the laconic quality of titles. With “Memo Grisaille,” though, it wasn’t my intention to trivialize this art-historical term. I simply like the combination of the words in terms of their sound, and the piece has something fragile and searching about it, like a memory that only becomes sharp and distinct in certain moments. So, with each title, there is an association that relates to the mood of the piece—with it or against it. ACL: Your previous album already explored a sense of joy derived from electronic sound interactions. Considering the track title themes, I think the argument can be made that there’s a humorous undercurrent in Der Saal tobt – there’s a philosophical perspective that says, basically, that it’s funny when things act like persons, but also the other way around. As the album’s automaton furiously fumbles around, we could be inspired to laugh: have you ever thought of experimental electronic music as possibly funny? Would you see a role for humor within your work, in the past, now, and in the future? EO: Experimental electronic music can be fun, sure. But so far, I haven’t gotten that feeling from this album. Then again, maybe I’m just missing something because I wasn’t sitting at the instruments or in front of the computer laughing while making it. Maybe it’s already fun when something unexpected happens. The staging of errors that make the automaton seem human, the unusual sounds, the friction in the gears, getting tangled up in the gestures—all of that could be interpreted as fun. For me, these are necessities, because I fear a well-oiled machine—and thus the predictable. And perhaps also I can’t take things, or myself, too seriously. So there may, after all, be a certain humorous distance, and therefore an unconscious influence on the tracks. But as the author myself, I can’t hear it. And that means humor would not have a defined role right now. If anything, it just happens, as it does in encounters with other people. For me, humor is indispensable there. In any case, I want to keep thinking about your question. There are quite a few inspiring examples in music, but also in visual art, that I would definitely describe as humorous. And maybe humor can get a more definite role in my work too. ACL: Thank you very much for your time, Sven. Is there anything else you’d like to tell our readers before closing this interview? EO: I’d like to thank you for these really challenging and intense questions. They went quite deep, and I found it very inspiring to think about them. Now I’m curious to know what it’s like to listen to the album after reading this interview—how it affects the way we perceive and contextualize this music. Especially since the album doesn’t necessarily need a strong conceptual framework, as it was created largely intuitively. Talking about it this way now almost feels like a kind of mental post-production, even though the music is already finished. And I consider it something special in itself to be able to release music like this, in the hope that there will be a few people out there who will actually listen to it and perhaps even find something in it. Thanks again for this opportunity.

items.body: Review by Fercandio46 — Contrasts define Aria for Labellum Tongues, the third album from the Houston, Texas-based band Kraanerg. From the opening track, "Amargosa Raga," the distorted guitar seems to clash with the violin, which follows its own distinct musical path, creating a unique sound. The band goes beyond the experiments of the Electric Light Orchestra, taking those ideas further by playing with atonality and, even better, finding a rhythm that makes perfect sense within that exploration. For amidst that chaos and rawness (qualities that are also classical in nature) there is genuine feeling.There is something hypnotic about the title track: the vocals, the band's frenetic rhythm, and Nat Bergrin's plaintive singing, accompanied by the violin and later turning operatic, evoke the most avant-garde side of Tom Waits. It suggests a cabaret where Fellini and Marc Ribot might coexist, yet it also feels as if the Mahavishnu Orchestra had gone punk.In "Blessings in Silk, Saffron, and Naran-Ji," the impression persists of hearing a classic piano-and-violin duo fused with a visceral rock band. When the saxophones join in and Nat Bergrin begins to croon, moving beyond the piano's traditional role, she makes another fundamental contribution, embodying through her voice that apparent contradiction between refinement and rawness, order and chaos, light and shadow. Maximilian Jacobs's violin evokes the classical style of cellist Erik Friedlander or the Balanescu Quartet, yet within a rock context, it takes on a weight that is more dramatic, more "pathetic" in the classical sense, grounded by Bergrin's earthy vocals.Anguloa Virginalis ("A Woman's Face") is a reinterpretation of jazz sensibility filtered through a personal lens, where the vibraphone provides the perfect touch. Then, Iron Sign of the Masdevallia begins, almost like a ritual, where, amidst wind and string arrangements as elaborate, complex, and sophisticated as Dan Britton's contemporary music, the spirit of John Zorn and a raw, rugged sound slip in, crossing a slender "Canterbury" bridge. And there are pieces of undeniable beauty and delicate craftsmanship that, underpinned by the solid foundation of drums and bass, take on a different texture. For the result is an orchestra of dark times, where the symphonic quality found within is progressive in a unique way.As with Dan Britton, the vocals aren't a strong point, but Kraanerg turns this into a virtue, treating the voice as just another dissonant instrument that contributes to the unique balance they aim for... and achieve. "Visible to the Wrong Faces" marks a return to twenty-minute suites, opening with piano and the band's signature bass synthesizer. A viola and a second guitar join in a crescendo, adding depth and lower-register resonance; syncopated, Eastern-influenced rhythms then take hold, while the violin and vibraphone toy with a near-pop melody that shifts tempo as Nat hums along, and a touch of Zappa creeps in, specifically the "cosmic sound" variety. The finale becomes epic, conjuring up even more unusual sonic fusions, a strange kind of epic where Gong and Renaissance might share the studio. Kraanerg offers a sensory experience that remains unaffected by time, as it unfolds outside of it.

items._cn_summary: 这张专辑建立在对比原则之上：失真吉他与小提琴各走各路，却形成独特的统一体。无调性探索中暗藏可感的节奏律动，混乱与粗粝中透出真实的情感力量。标题曲融合人声、狂热节奏与小提琴，兼具剧场感与朋克气质，宛如马哈维什努乐队走向punk世界。其他曲目中，钢琴与小提琴二重奏被嫁接至摇滚框架，萨克斯的加入打破传统角色定位；颤音琴为爵士质感注入私人视角；弦乐与管乐编排复杂精致，与Zorn式的粗粝棱角并存。二十多分钟的组曲回归，以低音合成器为底，叠加中提琴与吉他，东方节奏与近流行旋律交替浮现。人声被刻意处理为另一件不谐和乐器，为整体音色平衡服务。整张作品如同黑暗时代的管弦乐，内部蕴含的交响性以独特方式呈现其前卫特质。

items.body: Review by BrufordFreak — Recorded in London at Orange Recording Studios LTD. December 9-12, 1970 and then released early in 1971 by Global Records.A1. "Thursday Morning Sunrise" (11:38) not the opening I was expecting--ever--from a 1971 prog album much less a Jazz-Rock Fusion one. The deep, low, heavily distorted organ play sounds like Markus Pajakkala's baritone saxes and bass clarinet on his (memorable) 2017 Brutopianisti album! When other instruments finally join in they're all grotesquely distorted: Eberhard's wild (and virtuosic) electric bass, Siggi Schwab's Sonny-Sharrock/Arto Lindsay-like electric guitar, even the drumming/percussion work of Fred Braceful and Roland Wittich is wild. I wouldn't call this "Free Jazz" like something from Ornette Coleman, John Coltrane's post-A Love Supreme period, or Sun Ra's Arkestra, but a fusion of these with experimental sound explorations and, in the second half, the incorporation of sophisticated African rhythms with even some from the more avant-garde realms of Classical Music. I am blown away, incredibly impressed, and find myself incredibly entertained as well as fully enjoying this trail-blazing exercise in boundary-obliteration. Could this album have been a key food source for the inspiration of soon-to-appear bands like UNIVERS ZERO or AREA?--certainly this type of music (19.25/20)A2. "Lady Blue" (3:03) now, hearing this amazing song that combines Beatnik poetry-delivery musical formats with Classical Music choral traditions, I find myself asking whether or not Wolfgang, Eberhard, Siggi, and/or Fred were fans or progeny of George Russell's School of Esoteric Musics while George was a professor in residence at Sweden's Lund University. I absolutely love this! Another totally unexpected song that I find myself returning to over and over to try to fathom its creative scope. (9.75/10)A3. "Mellodroma 2a" (5:10) more choir appearances open this--from a distance--before Siggi's acoustic guitar enters playing with congas and double bass in what can only be descrived as a Folk Rock tune akin to something by Bert and John, The Pentangle, or The Incredible String Band. And the choir continues to make small appearances! These guys are amazing! The diverse interests and forms for their musical expression seems to have no bounds! Lite drums join in but it's the hand percussion that dominates with Eberhard's double bass Wonderful! Another song that totally took me by surprise and which lures me back again and again for repeated listens as I try desperately to fathom their thinking and desires. In the fourth minute there is a lull in which Siggi gets to show off a little more of his acoustic guitar skills, but then the rest of the band re-joins for a rousing finish with percussion and organ really bringing it (though no return of the choir). Wonderful! (9.333/10)B1. "Raga" (16:17) apparently Siggi Schwab had really gotten into a huge variety of World Music stringed instruments--and especially stringed instruments prevalent in India--like the but also zithers, psaltries, This track was actually written by Siggi, who is credited with a vast array of traditional, ethnic, and Indian stringed instruments on the record. Among the highly zither-like instruments he plays on the album and track are the swarmandal (credited as "surmandel") and the bulbul tarang. Siggi also contributed sitar, veena, tambura, and sarangi to the album's rich, psychedelic raga-rock sound. Eberhard, Fred, Roland, and Wolfgang do their best to provide inputs that they think will enhance, embellish, and not detract from Siggi's reverence for his Indian studies. I find the use of the full drum kit in the seventh through ninth minute to be a bit overwhelming and domineering to the Indian spirit being expressed but, it's a good awareness experiment and, fortunately, it ends so that the song can move into a new, more-percussion-centric passage--one that contains Eberhard's talking drum like bass play as well as a lot of intertwined and improvisationally-reactive percussion threads, gradually embellished by trumpet and, later, cymbal-crashing drum kit and distorted synth string sounds. Things quite down again in the sixteenth minute, leaving Siggi and his mates to finish the song with a thin palette of almost-incidental noises and percussives to usher Siggi's surmandel out. (By the way, Fred's drum play over this last sections is much more tasteful and respectful--much less invasive and brutal.) Another surreally-unexpected and eminently-enjoyable song that makes me wish I had been there--wish I could have been present for these practice and recording sessions as well as known these remarkably intrepid musicians! (28.25/30) B2. "Milkstreets" (4:15) a relatively unstructured melange of natural and unnatural (treated and electonic) sounds, many coming from African and Indian traditions. Interesting and historically significant (like the work of John Cage, Terry Riley, Herbie Hancock, Area and so many other adventurists). (8.875/10) Total time: 40:23YouTube provided me with three extra/bonus songs that apparently came from the same December 1970 London recording sessions but only saw the light of day (and a public awareness) on a 2008 CD release from the Long Hair label. They are also quite interesting and experimental, allowing for even more display of all the weird instruments that Siggi and Wolfgang had been playing around with. A/five stars; an absolute masterpiece of experimental and leading-edge Jazz-Rock Fusion. HIGHLY recommended and ESSENTIAL for any J-R Fusion and Progressive Rock fan.
items._cn_summary: 1970年底在伦敦录音的德语实验爵士摇滚专辑，横跨多重风格边界。开篇以深沉失真管风琴与扭曲电贝斯、电吉他构建前卫声响基底，融合自由爵士与实验声音探索，并引入非洲节奏与古典音乐元素。短曲将垮掉派诗歌吟诵与古典合唱传统结合，另设民谣摇滚段落，以手鼓、康加鼓与原声吉他为主线展开东方色彩的拉格段落，长达十六分钟。整张专辑展现乐手在民谣、摇滚、爵士、世界音乐与先锋古典之间的自由穿梭能力，编制不拘一格，文本部分对各曲目的编配细节与灵感来源做了细致解析。
