items.body: What happens if the sun disappears? The question lingered over the stage at Viljandi Folk Festival on the morning its closing day. Tell Your Birds brought it there, playing songs from a still unreleased record in front of a crowd for the first time. Kristīne Tukre‘s concert kokle carried the melodies, Vija Moore‘s balafon sat under them, Kärt Tambet‘s bowed hiiu kannel cut across both, and everything the three of them played ran through Simone Spampinato‘s processing. They sang in Estonian and Latvian at once, each keeping the language they grew up speaking. Some of the material comes from those same traditions, chopped up and rebuilt inside the band’s own songs. The rest belongs to no repertoire at all, written on the chance that one day it might. Straight after the set, in the last hour before Tell Your Birds broke apart for the rest of the summer, we sat down with the four of them not far from the stage, with a temperamental recorder giving us a hard time and cutting out every few minutes. Our chat eventually fell into the band’s own working rhythm: a burst, a stop, a burst. Tukre and Spampinato live in Helsinki, Tambet in Viljandi, Moore in Riga. They get a few days together, write everything in that stretch, then go back to their own cities until the next one. In the hour before they scattered, they talked about where a tradition comes from and what you have to know before using it, about melodies written for a time that has not happened yet, and about the syllables that decide which language a song ends up in. Tell Your Birds started with a student project. All four met at the Sibelius Academy in Helsinki, in different departments, and Tambet dates the band from there: “We came together as a band back in 2023, but back then it was a very specific project. It was Vija [Moore], who is our percussionist, her bachelor concert project in Sibelius Academy in Finland, where we all studied together.” The concert called for soundscape music written for one place and recorded in it, and the place Moore picked was a forest near Ērgļi, a village in Latvia. They hauled the balafon, the percussion, the violin and the kokle out among the trees and played there, birds and insects carrying on around them and ending up on the tape along with everything else. For Spampinato that set the method for everything after it: “it was the first project where we all get together and thought, we recorded everything outside. We tried to record the instruments as they were part of the soundscape in that sense.” That turned into Pause in Nature, then Carry on with Hope, out on 1 November 2024. One year later they wanted more room to move, and Tambet marks autumn 2025 as the turn: “to write together and to think of music more widely, maybe not so specifically as we had done before“. Moore had been waiting for it: “I like that with this new music, we got to put it all together.” There was a lot to put together. The four met inside one institution and arrived there from four directions, and Moore starts with the two furthest from folk: “Simone comes from sound art, electronics, different sound design type of experience and worldview. And then Kristīne comes from a contemporary composition and contemporary kantele playing. Also, Kristīne is interested in baroque music.” She and Tambet are the two who came up in folk, she through percussion, Tambet through singing and the violin. The spread is the point for Moore: “Each of us have a different genre outlook. I think it all comes together in our music, and it’s very interesting.“ Tukre’s own route ran through the classical kantele, though her instrument at home is the kokle. The Estonian kannel, the Latvian kokle and the Finnish kantele are cousins in one family of box zithers, and the family resemblance is where it gets interesting for her: “We have a very interesting phenomenon here in the Baltics and in Finland. We have these string instruments; they’re similar, but at the same time very different. They have different names, but we, musicians, try to come together.” The players of all three look across the borders to each other’s instruments. She did exactly that, a kokle player going to Helsinki to learn the kantele at the Sibelius Academy: “That’s how I got to Finland. I got to meet Viia, Gert and Simone, and we started the band.“ Coming together now happens across three countries, which turns rehearsals and recording sessions into an exercise of dates, plans and travel tickets, so they work in blocks: several days in one of the three places, everything at once, then dispersal. For Moore the two halves stay separate: “We just intensively get into the music for those couple of days, and then go back to our real lives.” Where those blocks happen feeds the music too. “I also think us meeting for intensive times in different places has played a big role in the music. Because when we have come to Viljandi, we get to see into the Viljandi life, and we get to see into the whole Estonian culture, even social culture. It plays such a big role of explaining what a tradition means. And then also going to Latvia all together, that was the missing puzzle pieces.” Estonia, Latvia and Finland have all had their turn. Italy is still waiting, as Spampinato points out: “We have not been to Italy. What a terrible thing!” The residencies have gone further than rehearsal rooms and taken the four into each other’s family homes, which Moore counts as its own kind of source material: “In our residencies, it’s very nice that we’ve met each other’s families because families represent culture in a whole other coded way, it’s something not explainable by words.” What comes back from those weeks is a songbook the band builds itself. Tambet traces the bulk of it to the four of them: “Most of the music is actually original music that we have composed together, or separately, but brought it to this group.” Folk melodies feed into it, and so do myths, texts and lyrics that arrive as words alone. Before using any of it, Tambet wants the origin and the original purpose clear: “there’s a lot of using a tradition in music. You have to be aware of it, and translating it to others. It’s highly important that we’re aware where it’s coming from and what the original intention behind that tradition is, so we can translate it into our own musical language.” The traditions Spampinato grew up with are not the ones on the table. He comes from Sicily, but his folk roots lie in Ciociaria, a historical region of southern Lazio: “My folk background is actually from Ciociaria, not Sicilian.” What he brings instead comes from sound art, electronics and sound design, where the tradition is the sound itself: “My background is more about sound. What do we do with every little sound?” Put that question to folk music and you get the music he admires most: “I’m really a huge fan of experimental French folk music, Sourdure for example, and I think we are trying to get into that.” In practice it means cutting material up and putting it back together: “What we use a lot is chopping and sampling, this kind of collage, things colliding. Sometimes they’re all together, sometimes we really like the contrast.” The same goes for how the four handle it on stage, where the play is in the treatment, not the tunes: “Maybe the songs don’t seem that playful, but how we manage our material is super playful. Viia is playing with four mallets [on the balafon], I’m on the synth and then the guitar. It’s collage in that sense.“ The same collage habit carries into the lyrics, starting with language. Sometimes the four sing three languages at the same time, like a group chanting together, each in their own language instead of settling on a shared one. For Tukre, that’s the point: “We don’t make these language compromises.” The words themselves usually start from folk songs and folk tales, which she reworks before they can be sung now: “The language tends to be quite archaic and doesn’t always fit with the world we live in. So we like to shape it a little and add some reference points we can relate to, but keep the original idea our ancestors had in their folk songs.” The shaping mostly falls to her, in Spampinato’s words “the poet of the band“. A song’s meaning is often sketched in English first, but the language it ends up in is chosen by ear, and for Moore sound decides it: “We’re a lot based on the sound, so what sound are we searching for? That’s where the language plays a big role.” Syllable counts settle much of it: “Some songs require Estonian lyrics, you can just feel it fits better, and some songs are Latvian. The number of syllables each language uses for one word can be different, so we use that to our advantage. How many syllables do we need? And just the pure phonetics of it.” Their latest single, “pa saulei”, is written and sung in Latvian and takes the idea down to a single word. Saule is sun, pasaule is world, and pa saulei means following the sun. Moore sums up the trick: “If you add these little syllables before and after it, it can change the meaning.“ “pa saulei”, like everything they put out, never leaves the band’s hands. The four handle the engineering, mixing and visuals themselves, and for Spampinato that’s the most independent way to work: “We do everything by ourselves: recording, mixing, visuals. It’s holistic, even though I don’t like the word. It’s maybe the most independent thing you can do, just do everything.” The setting shifts every time. Their debut was made outdoors in Ērgļi, a village in Latvia, with the instruments caught as part of the surrounding soundscape. The follow-up, due in April 2027, moves indoors to Moore’s house and home studio: “We think we need that kind of closeness, but still the comfort.” The shift is deliberate: “I don’t know what the next album will be, probably in a spaceship. But every time we try to come up not only with new music, but with a new way of approaching it.“ That album, due in April 2027, will carry the material they played at Viljandi Folk, and a single built on a traditional Estonian horn melody comes first, this September. A short tour follows in November, with Helsinki confirmed for 20 November as part of the Global Club Nights series, then release concerts in April in Latvia, Estonia and, they hope, Helsinki again. For anyone hearing them for the first time, the band’s own introduction says it best: “Tell Your Birds is a four-person music collective of musicians from Latvia, Estonia and Italy. We play our original compositions with collages of Estonian, Latvian and Italian traditional folk melodies and archive recordings and texts.“     Tell Your Birds released "pa saulei" in June, with the album due in April 2027 and everything in between turning up on their Instagram       The post Interview: Tell Your Birds – Writing a Tradition for Later (September 2026) appeared first on Rhythm Passport.

items._cn_summary: 这是一篇关于乐队Tell Your Birds在Viljandi民谣音乐节演出后的采访实录。该乐队由四位在赫尔辛基西贝柳斯学院相识的音乐家组成，分别来自爱沙尼亚、拉脱维亚和意大利，居住地分散于赫尔辛基、维尔扬迪和里加。他们将波罗的海传统乐器如kokle、balafon和hiu kannel与电子声音处理结合，用爱沙尼亚语和拉脱维亚语双语演唱，在数日的集中创作期后回到各自城市继续打磨素材。乐队最初的学生项目将乐器置于拉脱维亚森林中进行实地录音，捕捉鸟类与昆虫的环境声，将乐器视为声景的一部分，这一方法延续到后续作品中。新专辑试图突破以往较为限定的框架，给音乐更大的展开空间。他们在采访中探讨了传统的来源与使用边界、为尚未到来的时代谱写的旋律，以及音节如何决定一首歌最终属于哪种语言。

items.body: On the cotton candy sky Written every moment of life For all eternity Wonder why we are even alive Some records come from a scene, some from a city, and some seem to come from that ugly five-minute interval after you have stared at your phone too long and suddenly hate civilization. Faded Flowers, the latest album from Turkish Darkwave duo Ductape, belongs to the third category. It looks around at modern life: crowded rooms, digital selves, obedient routines, private disintegration, and finds a species that has become astonishingly good at maintaining appearances while quietly running itself into the ground. Çağla Güleray and Furkan Güleray formed Ductape in 2019 in Istanbul, where their mix of post-punk, darkwave, Turkish and English lyrics quickly carried them well beyond the usual underground boundaries. Four albums and two EPs later, they have relocated their creative base to France. Geography changes; the unease travels well. On Faded Flowers, that unease has acquired a larger target. The title gives you the central image without turning it into homework: people as flowers left too long beneath bad light, drained by repetition, expectation, isolation, and the exhausting business of becoming whatever the surrounding machinery finds acceptable. You can hear that pressure everywhere. The basslines have the cold discipline of public transport at six in the morning. Synthesizers cut through with little sympathy. Furkan’s guitar keeps finding ways to sound agitated without becoming decorative, sometimes stalking around Çağla’s voice, sometimes answering it, sometimes scraping at the walls. Çağla’s magnificent voice remains the great destabilizing force in Ductape. She can sound detached enough to frighten you, then suddenly let some exposed nerve show through before the song has time to make a ceremony of it. There is very little comfort in that delivery, which suits an album concerned with the absurdity of living among millions of people and still feeling marooned. That particular contradiction runs all through Faded Flowers. Everyone is visible now. Everyone is reachable. Everyone is encouraged to construct a public version of themselves, polish it, post it, improve it, defend it, sell it, then wake up tomorrow and do the same miserable maintenance all over again. Somewhere along the line, identity became administrative labour. Ductape sounds thoroughly fed up with the arrangement. The album keeps circling the false authorities people submit to without necessarily believing in them: social roles, digital identities, manufactured ideals, systems of power, inherited expectations, all those little invisible rules that become oppressive mostly because nobody remembers agreeing to them. There is anger in these songs, but also exhaustion, and the exhaustion may be more interesting. Rage still assumes you have energy to spare. Fine considers one dubious convenience of hitting bottom: at least you can stop pretending the view is lovely. The album’s first single follows a collapse through pain and disorientation toward an unexpected sense of ownership, as Çağla finds a place for herself inside the very circumstances that have undone her. A steady bassline and luminous synthesizers carry her weary composure, giving that uneasy acceptance room to develop. There is something wonderfully suspect about feeling comfortable down there, and the song lets the suspicion sit beside the relief. Within an album preoccupied with keeping up appearances, surrendering the performance becomes its own small freedom. The accompanying black-and-white video turns that process into a homemade alchemical experiment. Filmed at Misuc in Ankara, it casts the duo as silent-film experimenters collecting ingredients and tending a potion among curious specimens. Ductape handled the direction, styling, and production, with camera work by Mert Yalçın and editing by Çağla Güleray. Its antique laboratory makes an apt workshop for two people attempting to assemble another version of themselves. Standout track Obscure moves with a bassline so blunt and heavy it seems capable of carrying the song by itself, while Furkan Güleray’s distorted guitar keeps worrying at the edges, leaving abrasions rather than decoration. Synths hang overhead with an icy, almost antiseptic quality, giving the music the uneasy stillness of a room where something unpleasant has already been said. Çağla Güleray sings in English, her low register remarkably composed as she picks through disillusionment without dressing it up for sympathy. That restraint makes the words hit harder. Stolen light, dead idols, resentment calcified through repetition, the dull vacancy that follows years of believing in something that eventually reveals itself as another instrument of control: Obscure gathers these ideas until the song begins to feel less like despair than the slow recognition of how thoroughly faith can be exploited. There is damage here, certainly, but also the uncomfortable clarity that comes when the old explanations have finally stopped working. Its Berlin performance video brings that severity onto the stage. Directed by Altay Erlik, with cinematography by Emrah Celik and laser animation by Peter Isachenko, the clip concentrates on the duo’s physical presence, giving the song’s accusations the directness of an encounter across a crowded room. On Gölgesiz, the effort of continuing becomes almost physical. Sung in Turkish, the album’s second single carries accumulated sorrow through persistent drums and guitar figures that seem caught in the same argument with themselves. Çağla keeps her delivery measured, making fatigue audible through the weight she gives each phrase. The rhythm maintains its appointment with the next bar while the person inside it struggles to find a reason to follow. That uneasy relationship between bodily momentum and emotional depletion gives the song its force, extending the album’s concern with lives organised around obligations that have outlasted their meaning. Made during Ductape’s Latin American tour, the monochrome DIY video places Çağla against expanses of water and open space, her figure often reduced to a silhouette. Visual distortions make her outline appear unstable, as though even occupying a body has become difficult work. The images give the song’s isolation a scale that the surrounding emptiness only enlarges. Faded Flowers gains its pull from the sense that decay is something social as much as personal. The individual breaks down because the surrounding structure is already cracked. The city keeps moving. The screen keeps glowing. The machine keeps asking for another password. Somewhere inside all that, a person still has to decide who they are. Ductape leave that question open, with the bass still moving underneath it. Listen to Faded Flowers below and order the album here. Faded Flowers by Ductape To celebrate the album release, Ductape have announced headline shows and festival dates across Europe well into 2027. items._cn_summary: 土耳其双人组合Ductape的专辑《Faded Flowers》以暗潮与后朋克为骨架，贝斯线条冷峻如早班公交，合成器锋利切入，吉他游走于躁动与克制之间。女主唱Çağla的声音是全专核心，时而疏离得令人不安，时而突然暴露脆弱神经，演唱方式拒绝提供慰藉。专辑主题围绕现代生活的缓慢衰败展开：拥挤的公共空间、数字化的自我建构、服从性的日常节奏，以及身份沦为行政劳动的荒诞感。歌曲审视人们屈服却并不真正相信的虚假权威——社交角色、制造出的理想、继承而来的期待。整张作品弥漫着疲惫多于愤怒的情绪，承认到底部反而省去了继续维持体面的力气。土耳其与法国地理之间的位移为创作带来跨国视角，土耳其语与英语双语歌词拓宽了文本层次。

items.body: Our third iteration of the " Sculpting Silence " series, brings us to France, for a trio with Alexandra Grimal on saxophones, voice, harmonium, nōkan, shakuhachi, Naoto Yamagishi on percussions and Alexandre Saada on piano and harmonium. The title, Marée Basse , is French for “low tide”: the moment when the sea withdraws, leaving behind a wide, empty stretch of beach scattered with shells, tiny creatures, and fragments the waves have carried ashore. The music evokes much the same landscape. It takes this open space for granted, allowing the notes of saxophone, piano, and percussion to appear sparsely, sometimes only for brief moments before disappearing again. All three musicians are minimalists, deeply attentive to the overall sound yet reluctant to impose themselves upon it, as though the tones themselves should determine whether, and when, they wish to interact. Every sound feels tender and fragile, unobtrusive and gentle—and often completely absent. Silence is not merely the space between the notes; it is an essential part of the music itself. This is particularly striking in the thirty-minute second track, where, roughly halfway through, there is almost a full minute of near silence, with only faint crackling sounds barely audible in the background. When the music gradually returns, the instrumentation has subtly shifted: the harmonium introduces a handful of sustained tones, joined by Grimal's wordless singing, equally elongated and sensitive. Towards the end of the piece, the sound becomes fuller and more agitated, as though a sudden gust of wind were stirring the waves and awakening the distant cries of seagulls. Once again, silence plays an essential role in this music, much as it does in Japanese art, which has fascinated Grimaldi in recent years. Here, absence is not a lack but a presence of its own—a space in which the smallest sounds can emerge, linger for a moment, and then quietly disappear. Enjoy! Listen and download from Bandcamp . items._cn_summary: 这张专辑以法国为背景的三重奏为核心，使用萨克斯、人声、簧风琴、日本能管与尺八、钢琴和打击乐器构建出极度克制的声响景观。整体概念围绕"低潮"展开：音乐在广阔留白中稀疏出现，音符如潮水退去后散落的贝壳与碎片般短暂显现便消失。三位演奏者均倾向于极简主义，主动让出空间，使寂静本身成为音乐结构的核心。第二首三十分钟长曲中段出现近一分钟近乎完全的沉默，仅有微弱底噪，随后由簧风琴持续音和无词人声缓慢回归，结尾处声场渐趋饱满。日本艺术中"空"的美学理念渗透其中，将缺席转化为一种独立的存在形式，让最细微的声音得以浮现、停留、消散。

items.body:
This column is a loose gathering of recordings – two duos, two quartets – that might define a certain frontier, a degree of meaning in improvised interactivity spreading over 12 years. At times, the combination of close listening and simultaneous writing (the only way I can find to describe this music) results in verbal collisions that may be elusive in meaning, but they may also legitimately represent some of the transformative complexity and overlapping visions arising in these works of essentially collective invention. Though one of these recordings is more than a decade old, they may represent a kind of perpetual edge.

Certain musics can pass through walls of custom, identity, and meaning, assuming unknown shapes, escaping any strict verbal denotation, meaning becoming at once plastic and ineffable. Such music cannot be analyzed or described successfully, such failed exercises, however, perhaps contributing to both its mystery and its beauty, music that might suggest a hymn from an unknown culture, possibly disappeared, to an unknown deity, possibly deceased. In collectively improvised music, the role of the listener is paramount: assembling, collecting, composing ... At the same time, however, no interpretation is more privileged than another. These particular recordings are by musicians who can create dreams in sound. Some will imagine mills or factory floors, tuned to and amplifying unimaginable inventions of human industry. Empathy contributes a mutating, transformational soundscape. These are musics that create uncommon space.

Die Dritte Ebene (45 rpm LP, NiVuNiConnu, nvnc-lp062) by Emilio Gordoa and the late Sven-Åke Johansson might initially seem exotic. Ultimately, it’s not. It’s work of perfect transparency, that is, a view of whatever one hears as the other side of anywhere. The cover offers two titles, DIE DRITTE EBEN or EL TERCER NIVEL, “the third level,” in German or Spanish, with each phrase written with the “E”s written as reversed 3s. The phrase arises in Gordoa’s brief description appended to the Bandcamp page: “We were discussing how our music moves as if in parallel lines, and how after a while something third will emerge from it, almost like a ghost. It is something I find almost mystical: how this third level manifested itself in our playing without us thinking about it.”

Reminiscent of Johansson’s previous NiVuNiConnu release, Tea Time, with Nicholas Bussmann and Yan Jun, the music hints at Erik Satie’s Furniture Music, somehow constituting a radical background music that enhances consciousness, the special resonance of repeated materials creating a trance-like, near-ecstatic state, a reflective consciousness that rises between the parts created by Johansson and Gordoa, illuminating as well as hypnotic. Die Dritte Ebene, from August 26, 2023, points to an ineffable quality – a kind of trance, a kind of lift, a spectral point of attention that is produced in a listener’s collaboration with the close echoes, tight resonance and metallic rattle of Johansson’s snare, the reeds of his accordion, and the glassy ring of Gordoa’s vibraphone, glowing like light in sonic form. The shared insistence and simultaneity of Johansson and Gordoa’s work consistently expands what is essentially a minimalist musical environment, concluding with a strange abstraction of accordion and vibraphone that might suggest a kind of musical haunting.

Nate Wooley and Seymour Wright recorded About Trumpet and Saxophone in 2012, appearing on the Fataka label in 2013. While that release was unquestionably radical, its forthcoming successor, recorded in 2025, About Saxophone and Trumpet (Relative Pitch) takes a very different initial tack, opening with a deconstruction of the romantic ballad “The Midnight Sun,” composed by Lionel Hampton and Sonny Burke in 1947, recorded initially as an instrumental, with sufficient melodic grace to have lyrics later added by Johnny Mercer, spurring recordings by June Christy, Ella Fitzgerald, and Carmen McRae. Here the melody is clearly audible through a series of gasps, honks, and shattered, incomplete phrases, a nod to tradition that rapidly expands, becoming increasingly inclusive.

There follows “Experiment Four,” an extended dialogue which includes some of the strangest sounds ever emitted by saxophone and trumpet, often coming from very different positions in the sound spectrum. The fourth track, “Untitled,” is genuinely conversational, though the conversation is conducted in assorted bleats and blasts. Each musician is repeatedly triggered by the other’s material, whether pinching their sound inward, or adapting a radical extroversion. Music here will stand in for complex human relationships and perceptions, a sound store evolving to mark the impact of events in one’s daily life, worlds for which artists have long been refining their techniques and perceptions. As our descriptive apparatus daily fails before global events, our key artists stretch the elements. In that sense, call it modern syntactical practice or a soundtrack to Guernica, but the expressive range in which Wooley and Wright here operate seems perfectly in keeping with the daily news. Meanwhile, the inner tunings and sustained tones, even their matching fast vibratos suggest the development and synergy of an expressionist language. Sudden shifts will swiftly resemble elegant balladry of yore, echoes of that “Midnight Sun.”

While the Wooley/Wright duet recalls Fataka, Trevor Brent’s remarkable label – “‘dedicated to releasing recordings of small group and solo improvisations with a particular interest in situations where a common musical language has not yet fully emerged” – has become active again, releasing Parallels & Diagonals by a quartet from the label’s earlier period, 14th July 2014 at Cafe Oto, in which Wooley and Wright appear in a quartet with two percussionists active since the dawn of English free improvisation, Paul Lytton and Eddie Prévost. Contrary to Brent’s explanation of the label (and a genuine generational difference: the percussionists had discographies before the wind players were born), the four musicians seem so closely attuned – each a genuine spontaneous composer – that they sound like they might have had a long history together. Parallels and Diagonals is 12-year-old music, but it sounds like it might be recorded next year.

The opening track, the extended Parallel A, sounds like a machine shop that has discovered free improvisation, shifting dramatically after a passage of silence shortly after the 15-minute mark. The sounds suggest a light roll on a kettle drum, a brush on a cymbal, the sound of air pushed delicately through a trumpet. This notion of interiority marks the collective passage of these musicians, finding a terrain at once both barely imagined and yet a defining part of the human condition. In Diagonal A, fundamental gestures, like air squeezed through a metal tube, take on their own significance, behaving like Buddhist mudras, invoking fundamental gestures and symptoms of human life, murmurs, signs, abrasions. Diagonal B’s rapid actions and continuous overlapping suggest activity so closely attended by the musicians that it might follow a score in which the pauses might be carefully accounted, floating among a delicately bowed cymbal, other sounds that cannot be identified, and some that shimmer around audibility.

foam and mesh (Fundacja Słuchaj Records) by the B:A:N:S BAND is the work of pianist Sophie Agnel, saxophonist John Butcher, bassist Pascal Niggenkemper, and percussionist Ståle Liavik Solberg, recorded at the 2024 ArtAct Festival in St. Johann, Austria. While it’s the only grouping here with a conventional instrumental grouping, the orientation of the musicians will ensure that there is nothing resembling convention in the ways that the instruments are utilized.

foam and mesh I is clearly the main event, a 35-minute dialogue in which four of the most skilled spontaneous composers put together a dense weave of sonic events, with nothing predictable, yet everything interlocking. Tension curves are developed with astonishing power, each member of the quartet seemingly pursuing a unique and independent path, yet everything contributing to an astonishing rhythmic taffy-pull in which every part contribute to a compound and original overall momentum. This complex relationship will sustain through numerous group movements, whether slow balladic ruminations with isolated knocks and flurries or a sudden tense wedding of trembling oscillations, all four musicians regularly finding distinct timbres. The relatively brief foam and mesh II initially foregrounds Agnel’s piano, her focus initially on brief, isolated, tight-knit clusters with abstract flurries from Niggenkemper’s bass and the randomizing knitwork of Liavik Solberg. When Butcher initially enters on soprano saxophone, the random patterns generally coalesce into a continuous stream of different rhythms and complementary densities before the work’s ultimately gradual disappearance.
items._cn_summary: 这篇乐评汇集了四张跨越十二年的即兴录音，涵盖两组二重奏与两组四重奏，探讨集体即兴中的近距离倾听与同步写作。Gordoa与已故Johansson的二重奏以打击乐与人声交织出冥想般的'第三层'——一种从平行运动中涌现的幽灵般存在，呼应Erik Satie的家具音乐理念，在重复素材的共振中构建催眠与出神状态。整体音乐呈现难以言说的流动性，跨越习俗、身份与意义的边界，强调听者作为主动参与者的角色。NiVuNiConnu作为欧洲小众厂牌，专辑聚焦即兴中的透明性与神秘感，是欧洲自由即兴传统的延续。

items.body:
Gerry Hemingway leads a band of globe-trotters: German multi-reedist Frank Gratkowski whose recorded in the US often; pianist Izumi Kimura based in Ireland; Swiss bassist Christian Weber who’s recorded on three continents, crossing paths along the way with Yanks Oliver Lake, Ellery Eskelin, Nate Wooley, and Russ Johnson; Gerry himself, based in Lucerne since 2009.

In many ways Hemingway’s contemporary music mines his time in Anthony Braxton’s wondrous 1985-1993 quartet. The leaping staccato melody with asymmetrical phrases near the top of the 36-minute “Bau 4 Assembly” is one marker; another, the way that loose suite and the 23-minute “Slivers” use long improvised sections to tie together occasional scored episodes – not that Braxton was alone in that. And Braxton’s quartet prompted Hemingway’s duo with bandmate Marilyn Crispell, prefiguring his duo with Kimura in recent years.

On the CD, a six-minute Hemingway-Kimura improvisation is sandwiched between the long pieces, but I tend to cue up that “Third Story Variation” first, for its unbeatable interplay. The pianist and drummer catch and ride the same pulse, leaving plenty of air but also knowing how to fill various spaces along the way. Their timbral senses are fully compatible: her under-the-hood preparations tilt her sound drumward. They’ll set up a slow groove together, then she’ll use her other hand to play against it. It’s all very attentive and effective.

The longer pieces credited to Hemingway unfold like narratives, with discreet episodes, varied pacing, subgroup subplots, ways to build and dispel tension. “Slivers” is for trio, minus piano, Gratkowski leading off on squawky bass clarinet, tracked by Weber’s bass; the time feel is notably looser than the duo’s. A few minutes in, bass clarinet exits, and Frank’s re-entrance on disembodied wispy alto is placed just right: an instant orchestrator’s decision. Later there’s a section for low bass clarinet and arco bass in frictive unison under free drum rustle – suggesting Braxton’s love of the sub-basement, and the flexible trio dynamic of Gerry’s early/longtime vehicle BassDrumBone. But “Slivers” does slack off a bit between the scored tentpoles. There are times you wish the drummer would apply a firmer hand in a what-would-Billy-Higgins-do kind of way. One of Gerry’s signatures at the traps is a free-swinging–arms sense of relaxation, hitting the skins as if on the rebound, with some hits maybe dropped or delayed in transit. In the closing minutes, and on the closing theme, he can come off like someone who thinks he’s swinging harder than he is.

All four assemble for “Bau 4 Assembly” which makes up the bulk of the program. The venue Bau 4 in Altbüron, Switzerland was founded by folks in the timber business, and is located in their commercial compound. In tribute, Gerry and company play or use as beaters wood scraps retrieved from the workshop, notably heard around 10 minutes in, on a fast irregular clacky and texturally light colloquy which develops into something like pointillism with a groove (no small achievement) before flute and pedal-down piano soften things up. But not for long; in very short order, a scrapwood and piano gamelan. Midway, there’s a long-tone chapter with clarinet, and Gerry singing wavery lines into his cymbals or (says here) through metal objects, an odd effect he just about pulls off. (There’s a little Robert Wyatt in his vocal wah-wahs.) The composer and the quartet cover much ground. Elsewhere, a slow line’s melodic contours are subtly mirrored by the drums.

We won’t catalog every change-up or chapter, but near the end there’s a free-jazz blowout whose presence feels like checking a box – which is not to overlook Frank’s rapid multiphonic growls. (He’s got a great command of altissimo and pressurized reed textures.) Then they break into a loose brisk tempo, to frame that free-jazz energy. It arrives just where a non-drummer’s band would place a climactic the drum solo. Then a feint toward the Braxtonian head from half an hour earlier. A few staccato hits end things without a big fuss.

items._cn_summary: Gerry Hemingway领衔一支跨国乐队，德籍多管乐手Frank Gratkowski、爱尔兰钢琴家Izumi Kimura、瑞士贝斯手Christian Weber与Hemingway本人共同录制了这张现场专辑。Hemingway的当代创作深受其1985至1993年间参与Anthony Braxton四重奏的影响，不对称乐句的跳跃式主题与即兴段落串联谱写章节的手法清晰可辨。36分钟长曲将零散乐段松散地组织为组曲，23分钟的三重奏则由Gratkowski的低音单簧管起头，在松散时间感中穿插谱写与即兴。Kimura与Hemingway的二重奏段落以缓慢律动为基底，钢琴预制手法使音色向鼓靠拢，互动极为敏锐。乐队成员来自德、爱、瑞、美多国，演奏中还使用从瑞士Altbüron木工作坊拾来的木块作为打击棒，融入场地物质材料。长篇作品作为叙事体展开，各乐章节奏多变，乐器编配精到，但评论指出部分过渡段落略显松散。整体呈现的是学术爵士传统下的跨国即兴协作，融合欧洲自由即兴脉络与美国先锋爵士遗产。

items.body: Tomoyoshi Date and Stijn Huwels are experts of the minimal. Both musicians are known for their collaborative affairs – Tomoyoshi as part of Illuha, Opitope, and Melodia, and Hüwels with Norihito Suda, Danny Clay, and James Murray as part of Silent Vigils. Their releases have appeared on such highly-esteemed labels as Dauw, Eilean, 12k, and Home Normal. Both have a passion for minimalism. With hochu-ekki-tou (April 19, Home Normal), the pair conjure a long-lasting minimal atmosphere, running from the first second to the last drop. The pair complement one another to perfect degrees: both have a deep fascination for the art, maintaining the structure with delicate hands and soft tweaks which ebb, flow, and glow. They not only keep the music interesting, but they do it without jeopardising the drone’s sanctity, not wanting to deliberately interfere with its natural course and direction but adding tiny parts every now and then to the overall web of sound. It’s somewhat of a balancing act. The sound must be fed in stages so as to keep it from going stale, to add colour, shade, and interest, but add too much and you run the risk of decaying its minimal foundations. Patience is key. In some ways, minimal music is music of starvation. It requires the listener to go deeper, to go beneath its surface. Its lack of any real change is a crucial part of its self and its priceless beauty. It draws the musician towards it, pulling them into its sphere like a magnet. Then, and only then, does it reveal itself to be music of incredible depth, the opposite of a hunger, revealing well-fed, intensely satisfying music. The tracks are naturally long, as they need the space to develop and unwind, stretching their legs. This is a record of deep listening, and its slow-moving development never for a second stops it from being interesting or immediate. Minimalism involves a close-up shot, after all. There’s a nice parallel, a sweet contradiction, to the track, ‘ekki’, where sharp details come to the fore. Chips and scars come into view thanks to its high definition. A muted piano contradicts this proximity with a series of distant thumps, fingers treading over keys, coming from another part of the house and passing as if through thick walls. Looking at something in the distance will render it blurry. But something that’s extremely close can also appear blurred. The melody is like a whirlpool, slinking into the lower register and its inky depths, gradually expanding to take in more sounds. Adding gentle electric guitar melodies and the purifying sound of running water, coda ‘tou’ is tranquil and involving, bringing the listener into a secret place and helping to clear the mind of its worry-creases. The guitar’s tone is fragile, changing as it rings out. Together, the pair make exceptional minimal music. You wouldn’t want anyone else. www.homenormal.bandcamp.com
items._genre: minimal ambient / drone / contemporary classical / experimental
items._cn_summary: 这张专辑由Tomoyoshi Date与Stijn Huwels合作呈现，延续了两位音乐家在极简氛围领域的深厚积累。整张作品以一种贯穿始终的低限氛围铺陈开来，两人以极其克制的手法在持续音之上添加细微的声学元素，如同编织一张缓慢生长的声网。评论特别指出极简音乐的核心在于耐心与深度聆听——表层看似静止不动，实则蕴含着丰富的纵深层次。曲目‘ekki’以高解析度的细节著称，远处传来模糊的钢琴触键声，仿佛透过厚墙听闻的片段；终曲‘tou’则引入柔和的电吉他旋律与流水般的净化音色，将听者引入一片宁静而清澈的内心空间。整张专辑是对极简主义美学的一次精致践行，音符稀少却饱满，每一处微小变化都经过精心安排，适合沉静的深度聆听体验。

items.body: Palagoma is not only the first release from Nairobi-based label Cool Waters, it also marks the first time German-born, Kenya-based percussionist Sven Kacirek has collaborated with Ogoya Nengo and Olith Ratengo at the same time. Odd Okoddo, the duo of Kacirek and Ratengo, has been performing since 2018, but with the inclusion of the 83 year old Nengo, a singer from the eastern part of the country, there�s an added traditional depth to the music. A 2025 performance shows Nengo�s lifetime of experience singing Kenya�s dodo tradition around 2 and half minutes in (see below). Furthermore, her inclusion on this album allows her and Ratengo to toss the vocals back and forth as they reference their shared roots (Ratengo and Nengo live minutes from each other). Musically, however, the tracks are driven by Kacirek�s Buchla synth, hand percussion, and occasional kit drumming, which serve to buoy the voices without blotting out the music�s origins. Palagoma by Odd Okoddo & Ogoya Nengo �Bara,� for example, begins with the dime-store thwack of a repeated pattern, a stiff juxtaposition to the voices; yet, as the song rolls along, a 4/4 clink appears, then a burbling bass, and finally, what sounds like a xylophone. Layers of synthesized polyrhythms keep presenting themselves with a subtlety almost unnoticeable, until, by the track�s end, it feels organic, as if it�s all been underneath the two voices all along. Palagoma by Odd Okoddo & Ogoya Nengo �Sarah,� perhaps the album�s most intense track, features a lead vocal from Ratengo and tentative, percussive spittles from Kacirek. And while the technology never tries to overtake the vocals, it does sneak up and punctuate the track�s urgency, as edgy distortion sneaks in here and there just as Ratengo�s voice reaches its peak. The term �folktronica� has been bandied about as a way to house the type of music on offer here. In fact, exploratory collaborations such as Chouk Bwa & The �ngstr�mers as well as much of Kampala, Uganda�s Nyege Nyege label house sounds that might be �folktronic� in some way. What�s more interesting and important about this music, though, is how truly global so much of it is while maintaining a deep connection to Africa and its diasporic communities. The music on Palagoma , as well as much of what�s linked above (and available in countless other recent recordings) demonstrates a real willingness for cultures to respond to each other without trampling traditions altogether. Instead, roots become avant-garde and innovations become seemingly thousands of years old. Certainly the inclusion of an 83 year old traditional Kenyan singer only recently making her global debut as she tours with a duo whose instrumental voice is a white male saturated in electronic Kenyan rhythms demonstrates this blurring. The music this trio makes is certainly of the 21st century, but it�s often hazy, sparse, and open, keeping it from a quick sell-by date or confining it to a specific genre. Instead, it�s a beautiful example music as grace.
items.label: Cool Waters
items._cn_summary: 这张专辑由内罗毕新厂牌Cool Waters发行，融合了83岁肯尼亚传统歌手Ogoya Nengo的dodo歌唱传统与德国裔肯尼亚打击乐手Sven Kacirek的Buchla合成器、手打击乐和架子鼓。Kacirek与Ratengo组成的二人组Odd Okoddo自2018年起合作，本作加入Nengo后增添了传统的纵深感。三位音乐人来自地理上极为接近的社区，却代表了截然不同的代际与文化背景——一位年迈的本土传统歌手与一位深植于电子肯尼亚节奏的白人乐器演奏者。Kacirek的电子音色层层叠加合成复节奏，以几乎不可察觉的微妙方式衬托人声，从不喧宾夺主。曲目从廉价节拍器式的弹拨声逐渐引入4/4节拍、低频嗡鸣和木琴质感的声音，合成元素与原声人声最终融为有机整体。这种合作模式延续了Chouk Bwa与Nyege Nyege厂牌的探索路径，展现了跨文化对话中传统如何成为前卫、创新如何回归古老的多重可能性。

items.artist: Dorothy Moskowitz & United States of Alchemy
items.excerpt:
Known for playing with County Joe McDonald, and for her experimental sound band The United States of America, Dorothy Moskowitz came back in 2023 with United States of Alchemy and their well-received release,
Under an Endless Sky
.
In collaboration with avant-garde composer and filmmaker Francesco Paolo Paladino, and poet and music writer Luca Chino Ferrari,
Songs of Compassion
is eleven songs containing subversive and at times beautiful music, and richly evocative lyrics.
Francesco Paolo Paladi
items.body: Known for playing with County Joe McDonald, and for her experimental sound band The United States of America, Dorothy Moskowitz came back in 2023 with United States of Alchemy and their well-received release, Under an Endless Sky . In collaboration with avant-garde composer and filmmaker Francesco Paolo Paladino, and poet and music writer Luca Chino Ferrari, Songs of Compassion is eleven songs containing subversive and at times beautiful music, and richly evocative lyrics. Francesco Paolo Paladino and Luca Chino Ferrari | Photo by Maria Assunta Karini Songs of Compassion has two challenges for the listener. The first is the music, called variously avant-garde, ambient, modal, non-linear, and a few more. It is played mostly on pianos mixed in and out of the foreground, sometimes doubled, and sometimes out of phase, joined by strings, woodwinds, synth washes, and steely sounds. Initially disorienting, the music serves to remind us how locked our minds are to Western notions of harmonic movement. It speaks of alternative musical narratives much older and much further away. They are songs that subvert the song: more like Steve Reich than Steve Stills; more like Phillip Glass than Phil Collins. UNITED STATES OF ALCHEMY - Pale Wanderer At the same time, there are the poetic yet strikingly contemporary lyrics. �Pale Wanderer� talks about the fact that authoritarianism needs willing accomplices, describing what happens �When you make a deal with darkness.� UNITED STATES OF ALCHEMY (Dorothy Moskowitz, Francesco Paolo Paladino e Luka Chino Ferrari) by Silentes �Charlottesville� (written with the late Joe Byrd) evokes the time not long ago when torch-wielding nazis, proud of the metaphoric Ns on their tunics, chanted the antisemitic tropes paraphrased in Moskowitz�s words, �We�ll be one people, pure of race/No greedy throng could take our place� . Besides the overtly political lyrics, in the tradition of 1960s protest songs, there are also thoughtful meditations on mortality and our place in the universe. The message is high-minded yet sincere and direct. World weary and wise, Moskowitz�s voice inhabits the evocative philosophical lyrics with the authority of a skilled method actor. The melodies unfold like streams of consciousness, rising and falling, not following expected diatonic chord progressions, but honouring, instead, the value of each word. Moskowitz�s piano acts as another voice and sometimes a kind of Greek chorus commenting on the proceedings. The surrounding music frames, creates pulses and dissonances, and shimmers. The return of Dorothy Moskowitz with her renamed project has arrived in a moment quite similar to the times that spawned its predecessor. Political division, unrest, and uncertainty always generate artistic reaction, and United States of Alchemy roared back to life with their epic 24-minute opening track �Under an Endless Sky� in 2023, serving perhaps as an �In-A-Gadda-Da-Vida� for our times. Songs of Compassion continues to challenge how we think about our world. It�s music that defies the song form, while doing exactly what music is supposed to do�enrich the human condition. Find the artist online. The title track from the 2023 U.S. of Alchemy recording Under an Endless Sky by Dorothy Moskowitz & United States of Alchemy Further reading Cris Derksen - The Visit (Review) Tiny Sun - Vanishment (Review) Maria Ka - Di Mashin (Review) Further listening You will find a number of Dorothy Moskowitz's works on Race The Sky , most recently on Podgrammes #022 and #019.
items.label: Songs of Compassion
items._cn_summary: Dorothy Moskowitz 曾是1960年代实验乐队 The United States of America 的主唱，2023年与作曲家 Francesco Paolo Paladino 和诗人 Luca Chino Ferrari 合作推出专辑《Songs of Compassion》。专辑收录十一首歌曲，以钢琴为核心乐器，辅以弦乐、木管与合成器音层，声音被描述为前卫、氛围、模态与非线性，打破西方和声运动的传统逻辑，更接近 Steve Reich 与 Philip Glass 的简约主义美学。Moskowitz 的演唱以意识流方式展开，旋律不遵循常规音阶进行，而是服务于每一个词的含义。歌词具有强烈的当代政治批判性，《Pale Wanderer》揭示威权主义需要自愿的共犯，《Charlottesville》（由已故 Joe Byrd 共同创作）则直接引用新纳粹游行的反犹口号。整体融合政治抗议、哲学冥想与实验音乐结构，展现了一位资深音乐人跨越数十年的艺术延续性。

items.body: Tako Toki are like desert island musicians who, castaway without their instruments, were forced to construct their own. Lucky for us, they are as skilled in making instruments as they are in creating original songs with which to show off their handicrafts. Un Dimanche � Monaco is the band�s follow-up to their well-received debut, Hirsute Farfelus , with a similar mash of musical styles. Before discussing the music, we need to talk about their instrument closet. They really have built everything they play out of bric-a-brac, odds and ends, and rubbish. I�m not sure from listening which is which, but they call their instruments, in an incomplete list, tassofons, tilofons, and tubofones, clarinuts, didjerimou, and klarbass, and my favorite, kitchenofon. (I will refer to what I hear by the names of store-bought instruments that they sound like.) The most surprising thing for me was how accurate the instruments were to pitch and how good they sounded under the harsh scrutiny of modern recording microphones that have documented a rich, high-quality sound. UN DIMANCHE A MONACO - LP by Tako Toki They have also very effectively matched their choice of instruments with the style of music that inspires their compositions. Right off the top, �Yinitza� features a laughing clarinet singing a klezmer tune accompanied by bassoon for the bass, frantic two-time percussion, and the exuberant human yelps found on many klezmer recordings. As on this track, many tunes feature improvisations that show an impressive degree of musicianship. On the cumbia-inspired �Le Cuenta,� the characteristic flute carries the tune, augmented by a Spanish singing chorus, and remarkably rich-sounding Latin percussion. The title track surrounds us with afrobeat woodblocks, shakers, and rattles scattered around the mix. The melody is played on a marimba ornamented with bells and cymbals. Again, the lead player improvises over the tune and often against the beat with jazzy chops. The flute returns on the samba-inspired �Ambiguidade,� and on �Aksum� it traces a trance-like Middle Eastern tune reminiscent of a 60s TV spy-show theme. UN DIMANCHE A MONACO - LP by Tako Toki Full of fun and one of a kind, Un Dimanche � Monaco celebrates our universal love of rhythmic, melodic, and harmonic sounds and the varied, wonderful ways cultures have organized that love in what we call music. At the same time, playing on literal pieces of junk, Tako Tiko reminds us, as we contemplate many mall music shops filled with gleaming wood and brass instruments and countless unused guitars lying in closets, that musicians will always find a way to make music. Find the artist online. Further reading: Tako Toki - Hirsute Farfelus (Review) Terje Isungset - Glacial Poetry (Review)

items._cn_summary: Tako Toki 乐队以自制乐器为核心特色，用废旧物品手工打造出被称为 tassofons、tilofons、kitchenofon 等的独特乐器，每件都能精准调音并在录音中呈现出丰富清晰的声音质感。专辑《Un Dimanche à Monaco》延续首作的多元风格混融路线，将克莱兹默、昆比亚、非洲节拍、桑巴、中东风旋律等世界各地音乐语汇编织在一起。不同曲目对应不同的文化灵感：单簧管式的自制乐器演奏克莱兹默曲调，笛声承载昆比亚旋律，非洲木琴与铃铛构建 Afrobeat 律动。乐评特别指出乐队在乐器制作、风格匹配和即兴演奏三方面都展现出高超的技艺与巧思，以反工业化的方式诠释了音乐作为人类普世表达的本质。

items.body:
特集『ジョン・コルトレーン生誕100年』
音の見える風景　望月由美
NO. 341
（アーカイヴ）Chapter 16．ジョン・コルトレーン
2026年9月19日
望月由美

photo＆text by 望月由美
撮影：1966年7月、新宿歌舞伎町にて

 

1966年7月10日、日曜日の夕方、東京・大手町サンケイホール。日本初演直前の夕刻である。10日ほど前にビートルズの武道館コンサートがあり、TVの報道はビートルズ一色でコルトレーンの来日を告げるニュースは殆どなかったがサンケイホールの入場口へとつながる外階段には早い時間から当日券を求めるファンの列が出来ていた。午後6時半、コルトレーンは日本での第一声を放った。小豆色のスーツで登場したコルトレーンはおよそ、一時間半ほどを休みなく演奏を続けた。コルトレーンはほぼ肩幅ほどに足を広げ直立不動で一心不乱にホールを音で埋めてゆく。その音の密度の高さに会場は異常なまでの緊張感につつまれていった。ファラオ・サンダース（ts）を加えたニュー・クインテットのテンションの高さに圧倒されてアッという間にコンサートの終演を迎えたことを今でもはっきりと覚えている。当時のコンサートは二部構成で中間に歌が入り、最後はアンコールで終わるケースが一般的であったが、コルトレーンは一回のステージで全てを出し切るかのように間断なく音を埋めつくしステージを降りた。二日目のサンケイホールの演奏は『セカンド・ナイト・イン・東京』（impulse！）としてリリースされているが初日の演奏は未だに公開されていない。初日の演奏は自分が原体験したという贔屓目を差し引いたとしても日本で初めての音出しにコルトレーンの心境も二日目以降とは違って、より激しい求心力があったような気がしてならない。もう一度聴いてみたい気もするし、そっと記憶の中に留めておきたいようにも思える。今号のJazz Tokyoの表紙の写真はそのときの1966年7月10日、サンケイホールのコルトレーンである。

蒸し暑い夏の一夜、なんとなく胸騒ぎがしてカメラを手に新宿へと出向いた。多分「ポニー」の帰りだったと思う。予感が的中、歌舞伎町のコマ劇場近くの天麩羅屋さんでコルトレーンの一行とぱったりとであった。敬愛の念をこめて挨拶をすると、コルトレーンは優しい眼差しで迎えてくれた。落ち着いた静かな物腰に初対面とは思えない寛ぎを与えてくれる紳士であった。握手をしたときの大きくて分厚い手の温もりが未だに記憶に残っている。写真はそのときのコルトレーンとアリス夫人である。しっかりとレンズを見てくれるコルトレーンの澄んだ瞳は忘れられない。因みに二人の間からこちらを覗いているのはファラオ・サンダースである。コルトレーン夫妻は車で去り、他のメンバーは思い思いに歌舞伎町の闇に消えていった。私はつたない英語でラシード・アリ(ds)に語りかけ、歌舞伎町の街を歩いて「ピットイン」へと案内した。当時、「ピットイン」の司会をしていた相倉久人さんが出迎えて下さりオレンジ・ジュースを振舞っていただいた。ラシードはすぐさま、ドラム・セットに座った。実は、ラシードはエルヴィンよりも先に「ピットイン」で叩いていたことになる。きっちりとしたフォー・ビートを叩いたのにびっくりしたが、後にラシードのキャリアを知り納得した。

当時の日本のジャズ・シーンはアート・ブレイキーに始まりMJQ、H・シルヴァー、ロリンズ、マリガン、ブルーベック、マイルス、エリントン、ベイシー…と枚挙にいとまがないほど続いた海外アーティストの攻勢を傍目に脈々と息づいていた。コルトレーンの来日した66年は、前年（1965年）の暮れにボストンから帰国した渡辺貞夫（sax）が銀座の「ジャズギャラリー８」に出演、また新宿通りマルミビル裏手にオープンした「新宿ピットイン」にも出演するようになり、66年は渡辺貞夫を一つの極としてジャズがアメリカのものから日本のものになりつつあるという状況であった。当時の渡辺貞夫のグループには山下洋輔、菊地雅章、滝本国朗、鈴木勲、富樫雅彦、渡辺文雄など、錚々たるミュージシャンが去来し正に日本のジャズの一つの方向を示すエポックを築いた。新宿では歌舞伎町の「タロー」でも日野皓正やジョージ大塚等々が出演、「DIG」や「木馬」、「きーよ」などのジャズ喫茶の隆盛も相俟って新宿が日本のジャズの核となりつつあった。そして、それを決定づけたのがブレイキー、トニーと共に「三大ドラマー」の公演で来日し、不測の事情で一ヶ月ほど滞在を余儀なくされたエルヴィン・ジョーンズが66年の12月一杯「ピットイン」に連日出演したことであった。山下洋輔をはじめ、武田和命など多くの日本のミュージシャンがエルヴィンとセッションを重ね、新宿＝ジャズという図式が出来上がったのである。
その翌年、多分、1967年7月17日の月曜日の夜遅く、新宿東口二幸（現アルタ）裏の四階建ての小さなビルの三階。プレイボーイ誌の見開きヌード写真が無造作に貼られた狭い石の階段を上ってゆく。エレベーターは無かった。「DIG」の扉をそっと開ける。小学校の机のような小さな四角いテーブル、硬い木製の椅子。はがねの様に硬い音の塊がジャズの醍醐味を倍加してくれる。アーチー・シェップかマリオン・ブラウンか、その時かかっていたアルバムは失念したが、突然、音が止まった。一瞬の沈黙の後、中平さんの声がきこえた。“ジョン・コルトレーンさんが亡くなりました。たった今知らせが届きました。”中平さん独特のやや細身の優しい声だった。部屋の空気は止まった。再び「DIG」の音に戻るまでの10秒か20秒が恐ろしく永く感じられた。
「DIG」では中平さんが撮影された1966年のニューポート・ジャズ・フェスティヴァルのコルトレーンの8ミリ・カラー・フィルムの上映会がしばしば催された。無声の映像なので、中平さんは映像に『ヴィレッジヴァンガード・アゲイン』（impulse！）の音を重ね合わせるという妙案でDIGのファンにニューポートのコルトレーンを追体験させてくれた。
ジャズがもっとも過激で革新的であった60年代を牽引し駆け抜け、40歳という若さで昇天したジョン・コルトレーン。7月17日には決まって『Crescent』(impulse！) を聴くことにしている。

items._cn_summary: 本文以纪念约翰·科尔川诞辰百年为线索，结合望月由美1966年在东京亲眼见证其首演的私人回忆，描绘了科尔川与法老·桑德斯领衔的新五重奏在新宿歌舞伎町的演出场景。文字记录了科尔川近乎冥想般的密集声响如何在现场构筑出极度的张力，并穿插了与拉希德·阿里在Pit Inn即兴交流的片段。文章同时勾勒出1966年前后日本爵士版图的转型，从渡边贞夫回国到山下洋辅等本土乐手崛起，再到Elvin Jones在新宿驻演促成Shinjuku=Jazz格局的形成。结尾以DIG咖啡馆中Coltrane逝世消息的宣布作结，将个人体验与时代氛围紧密交织，是一篇兼具历史文献价值与情感温度的回忆性乐评。

items.body: Union Chapel in London stages “Vinyl Requiem 33.3” on 4 November 2026, a one-off return of Philip Jeck and Lol Sargent’s “Vinyl Requiem” to the venue where it premiered in 1993. Doors open at 18:30 and the programme starts at 19:30. Tickets are £18 plus booking fee through gigantic.com and are on sale now. The evening also marks the launch of a limited-edition double-vinyl reissue of “Vinyl Requiem” on Touch, the label Jeck was signed to from 1995 until his death in 2022. Vinyl Requiem 33.3 event details The programme centres on a full-scale projection of the 55-minute edited film of the 1993 performance, followed by a Q&A with people connected to the work and to Jeck’s creative life: Ghislaine Boddington (artistic director of the arts collective shinkansen), Mary Prestidge and Lol Sargent, the visual artist who created “Vinyl Requiem” with Jeck. Jon Wozencroft, co-founder of Touch, is also billed to take part. All profits from the night go to The Philip Jeck Foundation, a charity set up by Jeck’s family after his death to fund artists who produce experimental and creative work. Conceived by Jeck and Sargent at the start of the 1990s under the working title “The Death of Vinyl”, “Vinyl Requiem” was built for the 1993 Union Chapel performance from an 8-by-6-metre wall of 180 white Dansette record players, combined with 9 slide projectors and 2 16mm film projectors, according to Touch’s own catalogue notes. Three “Dansette operators” walked platforms in front of the record-player wall to swap discs live during the piece. The 1993 premiere was staged with the Institute of Contemporary Arts and also travelled to Ghent’s Time Festival in Belgium, later touring the UK, Austria and Belgium with support from the Arts Council. It won the Time Out Performance Award for Best Site-Specific Event in 1993. Sargent described the piece’s intent in an interview given around the time of its 20th anniversary: “What Philip and I created was an abstract expressionistic performance made in a very intuitive way to celebrate over 100 years of the mass public experience of the ‘record’. It was an art installation performance about a medium, using the medium.” Jeck, discussing the same period, was careful to separate the piece from nostalgia: “[Vinyl Requiem was not] a big mourning for records, I am not anti CD. It is a good starting point to mark this time of change from vinyl to other formats.” He also drew a direct line between his own practice and Sargent’s: “Lol uses his computer-controlled projectors as paint brushes. He paints with light which is similar to the way that I work with sound.” The critic David Toop, writing about the piece at the time, described its atmosphere in a short, often-cited line: “a mood of poignancy. Perhaps sadness is intrinsic to the medium.” About Philip Jeck and Lol Sargent Philip Jeck was born on 15 November 1952 and studied visual arts at Dartington College of Arts in Devon. After a trip to New York in 1979 introduced him to DJs including Walter Gibbons and Larry Levan, he began building compositions from old record players and vinyl in the early 1980s, initially scoring work for dance and theatre companies, including a five-year collaboration with choreographer Laurie Booth. “Vinyl Requiem”, made with Sargent for the 1993 Union Chapel performance, became his best-known work. Jeck signed to Touch in 1995 and released a run of albums on the label including “Loopholes” (1995), “Surf” (1998), “Stoke” (2002), “7” (2003), “Sand” (2008), “An Ark for the Listener” (2010) and “Cardinal” (2015). “Sand” was named the second-best album of 2008 by The Wire. He received the Paul Hamlyn Foundation Award for Composers in 2009. Jeck also collaborated with Jah Wobble, Jaki Liebezeit, David Sylvian, Janek Schaefer and Gavin Bryars, among others; his final credited recording was “Stardust”, a 2021 collaboration with Faith Coloccia. He died on 25 March 2022 in Liverpool, aged 69, following a brief illness. His family, including Mary Prestidge, subsequently established The Philip Jeck Foundation in his name. Lol Sargent is a UK visual artist who worked with Jeck on “Vinyl Requiem” from its conception, designing and hand-triggering the piece’s slide and film projections during live performances. He later oversaw the archival 55-minute edit of the 1993 film, released on DVD in 2013 with all proceeds going to The Philip Jeck Foundation. “Vinyl Requiem 33.3” reunites Sargent with the venue, the film and several of the people who worked on the original production, alongside the new Touch double-vinyl reissue of “Vinyl Requiem”.
items._genre: experimental / sound art / live performance / installation
items._cn_summary: 本文介绍Philip Jeck与Lol Sargent的《Vinyl Requiem》将于2026年在Union Chapel重演，并同步发行Touch厂牌的双张黑胶再版。该作品最初创作于1993年，以一面由180台白色Dansette唱机组成的8×6米唱片墙为核心，辅以9台幻灯投影机和2台16mm胶片投影机，由三名操作员在平台上现场更换唱片。表演融合唱片作为物质媒介的声音、视觉投影与现场表演，呈现对唱片百年公共聆听历史的抽象表达。文章同时回顾了作品的创作背景、巡演经历、所获奖项，以及创作者对媒介变迁而非怀旧情绪的立场。内容以演出预告与历史回顾为主，附带David Toop等评论者的简短引述，是一篇信息性较强的活动新闻与作品档案，但缺乏深度乐评分析。

items.body: Actress Radical Frame Making his return to the Ninja Tune label, Darren Cunningham practices typical elusiveness with doleful piano stabs amidst pounding surf and ambient textures Radical Frame by Actress Try to recall an Actress track and you won’t bring a melody or rhythm back. You’ll find only a noir sensation, the faint memory of wading through a city’s hazy silence at four in the morning, alone, but with something in the air around you that the skin registers before the mind does. A rusting Weltschmerz bleeds through Darren Cunningham’s music, dissolving evanescent motifs into lasting affect. Over twenty years into his career, Radical Frame sees the UK producer continue to explore music that resists forgetting. The almost preternatural allure of Cunningham’s first proper solo... The post Actress – Radical Frame appeared first on The Quietus.
items._cn_summary: 这张专辑延续了Darren Cunningham（Actress）一贯的模糊美学，拒绝提供清晰的旋律或节奏记忆，转而营造一种都市凌晨四点的孤寂氛围。评论指出其音乐渗透着衰败的世界感（Weltschmerz），将短暂易逝的动机溶解为持久的情绪效果。作品融合了忧伤钢琴碎片、重击的冲浪感音效和环境质感纹理，声音设计注重皮肤感知先于意识认知。Ninja Tune厂牌的背景下，这是他回归之作，继续探索抵抗遗忘的音乐形式。评论用文学化的noir意象描述听感，暗示作品适合在孤独情境中沉浸式聆听，其声音纹理具有先天的感官吸引力，但文章为节选性质，对专辑结构和曲目细节描述有限。

items.body: John X Belmonte’s Golden Lore understands a basic truth about goth clubs, doomed romance, and every terrible decision made after midnight: grandeur works best when there is something embarrassing hiding underneath it. The song moves with the confidence of a man walking into a ruined cathedral wearing sunglasses, fully aware that vanity and remorse have been sharing the same coat for years. Its synth bass keeps the floor moving with a steady, narcotic insistence, while Belmonte’s voice sits low in the mix, deep and controlled, as though he is delivering private evidence to a room that has already reached its verdict. The pitch-shifted echo curling around the vocal gives Belmonte’s delivery a doubled quality, part confession and part apparition, suggesting memory as a badly behaved accomplice rather than some sacred archive. Golden Lore keeps circling myth, beauty, regret, and self-invention, those old poisons that people pour into prettier bottles whenever reality starts looking cheap. The lyrics seem fascinated by how easily memory turns vanity into legend, and how legend eventually gets mistaken for truth. Golden Lore belongs to that hour when the dance floor becomes less a public space than a private reckoning set to a bassline. Belmonte gives the song enough romantic scale to make regret feel almost luxurious, letting memory dress its worst decisions in expensive clothes. By the final chorus, desire, vanity, and remorse have become impossible to separate, and the song leaves them circling one another beneath the club lights until closing time. As a dance track, Golden Lore has excellent instincts. The rhythm remains disciplined, the bassline stays heavy, and every element serves the forward motion. Nothing gets cluttered for the sake of drama. Then the chorus opens up, and this is where the song earns its black clothes. The melody is gorgeous without becoming sugary, large without losing its bruised center. There is a real sense of release in the refrain, the kind that makes a crowded room briefly feel communal even when everyone inside it is busy maintaining their own private disaster. You can hear why fans of Cold Cave, Drab Majesty, Then Comes Silence, and the Sisters of Mercy might find an immediate point of entry, though Belmonte keeps enough restraint in the arrangement to avoid drowning the song in borrowed gestures. The video takes a similarly direct route. Belmonte performs against images of a mysterious figure moving through a dark landscape with a giant ankh, the superimposition giving the clip the look of damaged film discovered in somebody’s locked drawer. The imagery is simple, but it suits the song’s obsession with memory, myth, and the ghostly versions of ourselves we keep polishing. Watch the video for Golden Lore below: Based in New York City, John X Belmonte is an independent darkwave and post-punk artist drawn to the romantic and cinematic possibilities of gothic music. His work pairs brooding atmosphere with rhythmic urgency, giving beauty and emotional intensity equal room within its electronic arrangements. Released September 18, 2026, Golden Lore brings that sensibility to its examination of myth, memory, and remorse. Listen to Golden Lore on Spotify here. Follow John X. items.body: Seduction gets complicated when one person knows the future, and the other is still getting accustomed to being human. Geneva Jacuzzi takes that imbalance to an entertaining extreme on Nu2U, a song she described in a 2024 interview with The FADER as an encounter between a primordial being and a caveman. Sex comes with a preview of the centuries ahead, including the suffering humanity has yet to invent for itself. Some lovers bring emotional baggage; this one brings the entire future of civilization. The Los Angeles musician and multimedia artist now gives that peculiar proposition a theatrical setting in the video for Nu2U, taken from her third album, Triple Fire, released on Dais Records in August 2024. Produced by Jacuzzi with co-production from Josh da Costa, the track supplies an appropriately crooked dance floor for an encounter across the ages. Nu2U bubbles and clangs with eerie, clamorous synths and foot-stomping percussion, making a persuasive case for synth music for cavemen. The occasional, emphatic keyboard stabs have an unmistakably prehistoric character, placing the track in the same mischievous tribe as Toto Coelo’s “I Eat Cannibals,” but if they ate edibles instead of flesh. Beneath that primal stomp, an intricate, melodic bassline curls through the arrangement, deepening the groove and giving its heavy steps a supple, sensual movement. Jacuzzi’s cool delivery, evocative of Erotica-era Madonna, presides over the gathering with a shamanic poise, her voice suggesting secret knowledge passed between bodies. The whole thing acquires a ritualistic pull, as though the discovery of electricity has given an ancient fertility dance some intriguing new possibilities. Directed and edited by Jacuzzi, with cinematography and art direction by Shannon Cornett, the video places its performers inside a set that recreates a work by artist Steven Arnold. Costumes are credited to Stacy Ellen Rich and Jacuzzi, with lighting by Tom Nixon and Fred Joseph. The official video credits make clear how many hands went into this compact, extravagantly strange production. Jacuzzi presides over a miniature theatre of cutout flames, suspended shapes, spirals, and stars, wearing an enormous geometric headdress above a pale costume punctuated with black circles. Her painted face and deliberate gestures suggest a celestial hostess who has been repeating this demonstration for several thousand years. Around her, figures pose in sculpted torso pieces, metallic-looking body paint, and elaborate accessories, turning the human form into another decorative element in the set. Deep blue lighting gives way to hot pink, red, and green, while stark monochrome close-ups interrupt the wider tableaux. Faces fill the frame; arms lift and bend; a crescent becomes a frame within the frame. The visibly handmade scenery lends the spectacle the intimacy of a toy theatre, even when its inhabitants look capable of rearranging the cosmos. There is a lovely absurdity to the scale of it all: the future of humanity appears to be under discussion in a cabaret small enough to pack into a van. Watch the video for “Nu2U” below: That meeting of pop music, costume, and performance has long been central to Jacuzzi’s work. Following Lamaze and Technophelia, Triple Fire brought her songs into sharper focus while preserving their appetite for strange characters and exaggerated situations. With Nu2U, another of those characters gets a stage, a formidable hat, and a captive audience. Triple Fire is available through Dais Records and Bandcamp. Triple Fire by Geneva Jacuzzi Geneva Jacuzzi is set to perform at The Chapel in San Francisco on September 19, 2026. She will be joined by EX-HEIR, Diesel Dudes, and Nick Moss, who will also DJ. Doors open at 8 p.m., and the all-ages show starts at 9 p.m. Tickets are available here. items.body: alarm!systemen self-titled Antibody Belgian newcomer alarm!systemen’s debut LP has a range of sounds and approaches which often belies a lack of direction or aesthetic, but that’s definitely not the case here. At large, the ten tracks on offer draw from long histories of coldwave and dream pop, but eschew slavish adherence to lo-fi nostalgia for its own sake. The classic Slowdive-isms of “Goes Again” are offset by clean, if minimal modern programming, and later on album closer “Void” serves as a reminder of how that act and other shoegaze giants found new life lifting from ambient electronics at large. On the more direct side, “Kapot” juxtaposes bricked-out synthpop drum programming with excellently reverbed guitar, and the dead simple but wonderfully executed dream pop nod of “BURN” shows just how far some wistful melodies and airy production can take you when they’re done with a measure of taste and restraint. Written over the course of five years, it’s perhaps not surprising that there’s this much variety here, but alarm!systemen’s real forte is in pulling it all off well enough to refresh familiar styles and serve as an example of how younger acts drawn to these classic sounds can rework and rethink them in their own manner. alarm!systemen by alarm!systemen Zataar First Crush CRVSH While based in France, the material released by producer Zataar draws from both her Morrocan and Belgian heritage. From the latter, you funky rhythmic electronics that hearken back to the New Beat era with a healthy dose of classic body music, where the former comes through in the melodies and instrumentation that reference North African folk music. Cuts like “Ali Sawtek” lean into the blend especially well, finding a swinging groove in the bass and drum programming, while Zataar’s vocals and the track’s melody are kept low and swirling in the mix, with big string stabs cutting through the thick reverb. As a contrast, “In the Lights You Call My Name” injects polyrhythmic complexity into the drum track, its belchy resonant bassline flowing beneath rich waves of plucks and pads. The cleverness in the arrangements really comes through on “Moments in Love”, which manages transitions between deep house styled rhythm programming and sections of Chaabi folk melodies, before combining them smoothly into a hypnotic whole. Far from a gimmick, it’s a fully realized approach that recognizes the commonality and contrasts inherent in blending multiple styles and genres, and then reconciles them handily.
